2026金融AI智能体落地新标杆：中原银行与中信建投最新实践启示
2026年6月，中国金融AI智能体落地迎来两个标志性事件：中原银行外呼营销智能体斩获”2026中国AI智能体领航者”奖项，中信建投证券”信谛听”智数平台1.5版本正式上线并率先在核心业务场景切换至国产大模型。这两条消息看似独立，实则指向同一个趋势——金融AI智能体的竞争，正从”模型参数竞赛”转向”规模化交付能力”的比拼。
趋势：金融AI智能体进入”可信交付”时代
截至2026年6月，中国已有近800款大模型完成备案，53.5%的银行已上线大模型应用（来源：2026年银行业大模型应用调研报告）。但与2025年的”试点潮”不同，2026年金融机构关注的核心问题已从”模型够不够强”变成了”交付够不够可靠”。
如我们在 《金融行业AI智能体落地指南》 中分析的，金融场景对AI智能体的核心要求是零容错。无论是外呼营销中的合规话术控制，还是投研分析中的信息溯源，任何一次模型”幻觉”都可能导致实质性业务风险。中原银行与中信建投的最新实践，恰好从两个不同维度回应了这一核心诉求。
中原银行：双引擎架构破解外呼营销合规难题
中原银行作为资产规模超1.4万亿的省属法人银行，拥有600余家营业网点、1.8万余名员工。其与中关村科金联合申报的”外呼营销智能体”项目，在2026中国AI智能体领航者评选中从众多参评项目中脱颖而出。
该项目的核心创新在于”通用大模型+SOP流程”与”业务微调大模型”的双引擎架构：
SOP强约束 ：通过标准作业流程（SOP）约束对话路径，确保外呼全程在合规框架内运行，从架构层面杜绝大模型”幻觉”带来的话术风险
业务微调 ：基于中原银行真实业务语料进行监督微调，大幅增强模型在存款、理财、个贷等场景下的语义理解和意图识别能力
人机协同 ：智能体完成客户意向初筛，高价值线索无缝转接至人工坐席深度转化
这种架构设计的关键洞察在于：金融场景不需要”全能”的AI，而是需要”受控”的AI。SOP相当于给AI画了一条合规的跑道，让它在这个范围内发挥最大效率，而不是自由探索。
中信建投：从”能生成”到”能负责”的AI落地标准
中信建投”信谛听”1.5版本的升级，则展示了另一条路径：以专业数据为核心壁垒构建可信AI体系。
值得关注的是，”信谛听”1.5率先切换至国产大模型DeepSeek V4并完成核心场景验证。有报道称，中信建投信息技术部门相关负责人在公开活动中对国产大模型能力与成本优势表达了肯定（具体表述未经当事人核实）。
“信谛听”1.5的核心升级包括三项关键能力：
自适应纠错框架 ：让代码自己改Bug，大幅提升策略回测效率
DeepTiming搜索 ：首次整合中信建投7000余篇研报，拆解为超10万个可溯源知识原子，用户提问20秒内获得附带原文链接的精准回答
多智能体协同研究 ：支持分析师团队与AI协同完成研究报告撰写
其中”DeepTiming搜索”的设计思路尤其值得关注——用专业审核过的研报框定信息边界，让每条结论都可溯源。这恰好回应了行业对AI语料污染的普遍担忧：高质量专有数据正在成为金融机构构建AI可信体系的关键防线。
金融AI智能体选型的三个关键维度
结合上述案例与当前市场供给（来源：2026年企业级AI智能体选型指南综合梳理），金融机构在评估AI智能体平台时建议关注以下三个维度：
维度 核心问题 中原银行方案 中信建投方案 合规可控 如何防止AI”越界”？ SOP流程约束+话术合规检查 研报知识原子+溯源机制 数据壁垒 AI是否基于真实业务数据？ 业务微调大模型+真实语料 20TB机构级金融数据+脱敏研报 国产适配 能否满足信创和数据安全要求？ 私有化部署+国产大模型接入 切换至DeepSeek V4完成验证 对于计划引入AI智能体的长沙及中部地区金融机构和类金融企业，这三个维度可以作为选型评估的基础框架。重点不在于平台功能多全面，而在于能否在合规前提下实现稳定的业务价值。
长沙企业的启示：金融AI智能体落地的”三先”策略
中原银行与中信建投的实践验证了一个核心结论：金融AI智能体落地的关键不在于技术有多前沿，而在于能否在合规框架下产出稳定的业务价值。对于长沙及中部地区面临AI转型的企业，建议采取”三先”策略：
先框定场景 ：选择容忍度相对较高、边界清晰的业务场景（如外呼初筛、文档处理、报告辅助），而非一开始就挑战核心交易系统
先建立标准 ：明确AI输出的合规要求和验证机制，确保每条AI结论都可回溯、可审计
先验证价值 ：通过小范围试点（如一个网点、一个业务条线）验证ROI后再规模化推广，避免一步到位的风险
如我们在 《2026国产大模型本地化部署成本实测》 中测算的，当前国产大模型的部署成本已降至单项目5-20万元的区间。这意味着即便是预算有限的中部企业，也完全可以在不盲目追求大规模投入的前提下，找到适合自己的AI智能体切入点。
结语：从单点试验到规模化落地的关键一步
中原银行的获奖与中信建投的升级表明，2026年中国金融AI智能体正在完成从”单点试验”到”规模化落地”的关键跨越。对于长沙及中部地区的企业决策者来说，现在的问题不是”要不要用AI”，而是”如何用AI”。从合规框架出发，以业务数据为基础，在小场景中验证价值——这或许是当下务实的AI落地路径之一。

X 上的 Rohan Paul：“Main takeaways from SpaceX’s earnings call today
> AI is now SpaceX’s biggest business: The Super Intelligence segment, which rents computing capacity to customers including Anthropic and Google, brought in $7.6B, nearly triple its $2.56B in the second quarter.
That made it SpaceX’s largest revenue source, ahead of the $5.2B Starlink connectivity business, with $608M coming from the newly acquired Cursor.
> SpaceX swung to a profit: Net income reached $4.4B on $14.6B of revenue, up 161%, against a $1.1B loss a year earlier and a $541M loss in the second quarter. Even so, SpaceX still showed a $413M net loss for the first 9 months of 2026.
> A SpaceX-Tesla merger is under study: Committees of independent directors at both companies are discussing a combination at shareholders’ request, and Musk said he is excluded from those talks as a conflicted party. He called a merger a good idea but said it isn’t certain, and any deal would need support from a majority of all outstanding Tesla shares.
> Musk sees revenue multiplying: Musk projected annual recurring revenue of $500B to $1T by the end of 2027. SpaceX’s own guidance is far lower in the near term, with $100B in annualized revenue by the end of 2026, based on December sales, and $33B to $37B of revenue in the first quarter of 2027.
> Spending is outrunning revenue: Capital spending hit $19.6B in the third quarter, $16.4B of it in the AI segment, and SpaceX expects $35B to $40B in the fourth quarter. Musk said SpaceX prefers short-term compute contracts because he expects each watt of computing to earn more as AI models improve.
> Musk is working from Memphis: Musk said he often spends 4 days a week in Memphis bringing the Colossus II supercomputer online, as SpaceX adds roughly 200K Nvidia GB300 chips a month. Compute capacity stood at 1.7GW at the end of September, SpaceX expects 2.5GW to 3GW by year-end, and Musk said he is confident of adding 10GW during 2027.
> Louisiana launches are expected by 2029: SpaceX recently announced plans for a $100B spaceport in Louisiana, and Musk said the internal goal is a first launch there within 2 years, while 2029 is highly likely, with launches at scale that year.”

items.title: 蚂蚁集团与 vLLM 社区开源量化推理内核库 Humming
items.title_en: Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference
items.summary: 蚂蚁集团与 vLLM 社区开源通用高性能量化推理内核库 Humming，仓库为 github.com/vllm-project/humming。
items.fullContent:
Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference | vLLM Blog
Menu
Theme
Table of Contents
Ant Group and the vLLM community are open-sourcing Humming, a general-purpose, high-performance kernel library for quantized inference. Humming offers the following features:
Broad device support : Supports NVIDIA GPU architectures from Turing onward, along with CUDA-compatible devices such as T-Head's Zhenwu 810E.
Extensive quantization support : A unified architecture supports diverse combinations of weight and activation formats for dense and MoE workloads, covering a wide range of integer and floating-point types, bit widths, and scaling schemes.
Strong execution performance : Significantly outperforms existing implementations from vLLM Marlin, FlashInfer, and DeepGEMM across many representative workloads.
Repository: github.com/vllm-project/humming
Background
As models and inference workloads grow, memory capacity, memory bandwidth, and compute costs increasingly constrain deployment. This is especially apparent in MoE models: each token activates only a subset of experts, but the full set of weights still needs to be stored. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671 billion parameters, with 37 billion activated per token. Quantization lowers the precision of weights and activations to reduce memory usage and data movement, and can also improve compute efficiency.
Quantization requirements vary across models and GPU generations. Common configurations include WNA16, W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4, where W and A specify weight and activation bit widths, and N denotes a variable weight bit width. Even at the same precision, schemes such as INT4 and NVFP4 differ in numeric format and scaling. Scaling granularity, scale representation, group size, and symmetric or asymmetric quantization further expand the configuration space.
These storage and compute savings only translate into lower latency and higher throughput with efficient kernels. Prefill, decode, and varying MoE expert loads place different demands on compute and memory. Kernels must adapt to these workloads while keeping conversion, dequantization, and scheduling overhead low.
Developing and integrating a dedicated kernel for every combination creates a growing maintenance burden. Each addition can require its own weight preprocessing, kernel selection, framework adapters, and tests. Optimizations must then be carried across multiple implementations.
Humming addresses this problem by separating quantization descriptions from execution choices and composing kernels from shared components.
General-Purpose Architecture
Humming's execution path has three parts: represent the quantized computation, select configurations for the hardware and workload, and compile a kernel from CUDA components.
A Unified Quantization Representation
Models exported by different quantization tools vary in numeric format, parameter organization, and weight layout. Humming converts supported export formats into the Humming standard format: a common quantization description with consistently organized weights, scales, zero points, and other tensors.
This representation preserves each scheme's quantization semantics while describing weight format, scaling granularity, scale data type, zero points, and secondary scales as separate parameters. Activations have their own numeric format and quantization settings. These parameters can be combined subject to format and hardware constraints.
For example, groupwise INT4 weights can be paired with BF16 activations. Low-precision floating-point weights with different scaling schemes use the same parameter system. This gives inference frameworks a common interface for models from different sources.
Tuning and JIT Compilation for Each Workload
The standard format provides a common representation across export formats. Preprocessing then validates parameters, pads dimensions, and repacks these tensors into layouts suited to the target kernel. Humming combines the quantization description with the weight shape, GEMM type, target GPU, and compute options to configure execution.
Three configurations describe the kernel:
Layer Config describes tensor shapes, data types, quantization parameters, and the target architecture.
Compute Config specifies the GEMM type and computation options, such as batch invariance and input scale layout.
Tuning Config selects tile shapes, pipeline stage counts, warp specialization, memory access, and MMA instructions. It also controls concurrency and scheduling; TMA can be configured per tensor.
By default, Humming selects tuning configurations using device-specific heuristics. It can prepare different configurations for ranges of input sizes and dispatch to the appropriate kernel at runtime.
Humming’s unified architecture makes it straightforward to tune execution parameters and select pipelines for different workloads. At small batch sizes, a multistage pipeline using asynchronous copies ( cp.async ) and MMA can outperform a pipeline built around TMA and UMMA. At larger batch sizes, TMA and UMMA can offer better throughput. Humming accommodates both execution paths within the same configuration and component framework, allowing it to select the more effective strategy for each workload.
Together, the three configurations specialize kernels compiled with NVRTC or NVCC. Compiled kernels are cached for reuse. Inference combines the selected kernel with the preprocessed weights and runtime activations.
Shared CUDA Components Across Formats and Architectures
At the CUDA level, Humming organizes task scheduling, data movement, dequantization and scaling, Tensor Core computation, and output processing into reusable components. It provides standard, warp-specialized, and dedicated UMMA pipelines. These pipelines share compatible components while using the dataflow and synchronization required by each execution strategy.
Each group of components handles a different source of variation:
Numeric processing handles quantization formats. Decoding and arithmetic components account for bit width, integer or floating-point representation, scales, and zero points. Dequantization and scaling are integrated into the kernel's computation.
Memory and compute backends handle GPU architectures. Humming selects data movement and Tensor Core implementations for the target architecture, using asynchronous copies, TMA, and multicast where supported.
Task mapping and scheduling handle dense and MoE workloads. Each GEMM type uses the appropriate scheduling logic. Scaling and bias addition can also be fused into the output stage.
JIT compilation combines these components according to the three configurations and eliminates unused implementation branches. A new format or architecture can therefore be supported by extending the relevant components. Improvements to a shared component benefit compatible configurations, reducing the duplicated development and maintenance of separate specialized kernels.
This CUDA implementation is lightweight and avoids heavyweight kernel framework dependencies, keeping JIT compilation fast as well. In our single W4A16 kernel compilation test on an H200 server with CUDA 13.4, compilation time dropped from 23.35 seconds for CUTLASS with NVCC to 1.82 seconds for Humming with NVCC or 1.88 seconds with NVRTC , with compilation caches disabled. This reduces the cost of preparing kernels for new workloads and makes iterative tuning more practical. Humming also compiles kernels in parallel during model warmup. In our tests, compiling and loading the kernels covering all supported M sizes for a single layer's GEMM takes only about 2–4 seconds , making it practical to prepare multiple specialized kernels before inference.
Performance Tuning Based on Device Parameters
Humming deeply optimizes kernels using both the GEMM configuration and device parameters. Quantization formats, matrix shapes, GPU instruction support, SM count, shared memory, and register resources all inform execution choices, turning the benefits of low-bit storage into practical inference performance.
Efficient W4A8-MXFP4 inference on existing GPUs. Architectures before Blackwell lack native MXFP4 Tensor Core support, and conventional W4A8-MXFP4 kernels can be limited by dequantization and scaling overhead at larger M. Humming addresses this with a fast MXFP4-to-INT8/FP8 dequantization path that converts MXFP4 weights into a supported compute format within the kernel. In this setting, the path substantially outperforms conventional W4A8 implementations at small M and approaches W8A8 performance at large M. GPUs such as H200 can therefore run high-performance W4A8-MXFP4 kernels while retaining the storage benefits of 4-bit weights.
Dequantization paths matched to each device. The same quantization format can benefit from different implementations across GPUs. Humming selects decoding, numeric conversion, and scaling paths for the device, pairing them with suitable memory access and compute pipelines to reduce instruction and data movement overhead. Shared components make these optimizations reusable across compatible dense and MoE kernels.
Extensive tuning controls with device-specific heuristics. Humming exposes tile shapes, pipeline stage counts, warp specialization, TMA, MMA instructions, CTA concurrency, and Stream-K scheduling. Device-specific heuristics combine GEMM shapes with resource constraints to balance parallelism, data reuse, and pipeline overhead, selecting different execution strategies as input sizes change. Developers can use the default configurations directly or refine them for particular models and deployment scenarios.
Results
Broad Device Support
Humming's unified architecture enables broad GPU support. For NVIDIA GPUs, Humming fully supports every architecture from Turing onward, bringing a common quantized computing framework to multiple generations of hardware.
The unified JIT architecture also makes it straightforward to extend Humming to other GPUs compatible with CUDA programming. Humming already fully supports T-Head's Zhenwu 810E, bringing its shared kernels and tuning capabilities to more hardware platforms.
The figure below shows the high-performance activation types supported by Humming on each device: types that can take full advantage of the device's peak compute capabilities. Some types omitted from the figure can still run through other instruction paths. For example, UMMA instructions on the B300 (SM103) no longer support INT8 computation, but earlier MMA instructions can still execute INT8 GEMM, with substantially lower performance.
Quantization Support
Humming's support for quantization types depends primarily on compatibility between activation and weight types. Its unified quantization representation and kernel architecture allow a wide range of integer and floating-point weight formats to work with activations at different precisions, providing flexible choices for model precision and deployment performance.
The figure below shows the weight and activation type combinations supported by Humming. Rows represent weight types, columns represent activation types, and checks indicate supported combinations. Together with the device support matrix above, it outlines the high-performance quantized computation paths available on each hardware architecture.
Humming also supports a special floating-point format with zero exponent bits, whose representable values match those of symmetric integers at the same bit width. For example, INT8 excluding -128 and float8e0m7 both represent integers from -127 to 127 . Weights in this format have the same activation type compatibility as INT weights of the same bit width. Humming automatically converts eligible symmetric integer weights to this format for faster dequantization.
The community has also uncovered two hidden capabilities in Blackwell Tensor Cores : native support for float4e0m3 and float8e3m4 , two special floating-point formats that are not exposed in the PTX type system. Humming supports these features across all Blackwell architectures, including datacenter SM100/SM103 and SM120/SM121 devices for workstations and personal computing. Both formats are integrated into its unified quantization and compute framework, providing more native compute options for low-precision inference. Rubin does not support these two hidden Tensor Core formats, so support for these native compute paths does not extend to Rubin.
Performance
The kernel microbenchmarks below, run by the vLLM community, measure GEMM performance with M covering every power of two from 1 to 8192. Kernels are fully warmed up and timed independently with a cold L2 cache, with a brief pause between samples. MoE speedups use the sum of Gateup and Down GEMM latencies. Each figure identifies its baseline, quantization formats, matrix dimensions, and software versions.
WnA16
WnA16 is one of the most versatile and widely used approaches to quantized inference. It combines low-bit weights with FP16/BF16 activations, reducing weight storage and memory traffic while making use of widely available 16-bit compute capabilities. This makes it suitable for many GPU generations and model deployment scenarios. The W4A16 family has attracted particular interest from the community and is a major focus of Humming's optimization work.
For dense W4A16, Humming matches or outperforms vLLM Marlin in most tested configurations, with substantial gains on several Hopper and Blackwell workloads. The figure below uses cuBLAS as a common baseline. At small batch sizes, Humming delivers roughly 3–4× speedups on several devices. As batch size grows, it continues to use the hardware efficiently, reaching approximately twice Marlin's performance on large-batch H200 workloads and more than three times its performance in some B300 cases.
These gains extend to MoE. Humming provides efficient Indexed and Grouped paths for workloads where tokens are distributed across experts and the amount of work per expert changes with the load. In the figure below, MXFP4 W4A16 on H20 and H200 reaches roughly twice Marlin's performance in several medium-to-large batch cases. On B300, the MXINT4 and NVFP4 paths achieve even larger gains at large batch sizes, with the Grouped path reaching approximately 5×. Results on SM120 and SM121 also show Humming outperforming Marlin and the corresponding FlashInfer implementations across a range of workloads.
Humming's optimizations also extend beyond W4A16 to other WnA16 combinations. Its shared dequantization and compute paths deliver strong performance for integer and floating-point weights at different bit widths, including INT1, INT2, INT3, and FP4 through FP8. The following figure shows broad gains across these formats at small and medium batch sizes, with the lowest-bit configurations on SM120 exceeding 5× the performance of BF16 cuBLAS. At large batch sizes on H20, multiple bit widths maintain compute efficiency close to BF16 cuBLAS. This gives models finer-grained choices among precision, storage, and throughput.
W8A8 / W4A8 / W4A4
With Hopper, FP8 W8A8 with blockwise scaling became a mainstream approach to high-performance quantized inference. Humming further improves this established compute path by optimizing data movement, scaling, and expert scheduling together. The left column below shows W8A8 results on H20 and H200. At small and medium batch sizes, Humming reaches approximately 2.6× and 2.5× the performance of DeepGEMM Contiguous, respectively, with competitive performance from both Indexed and Grouped layouts.
As more models adopt native MXFP4 weight quantization, converting the smaller weight footprint into practical inference gains becomes increasingly valuable. Humming addresses this with an efficient W4A8 path that rapidly dequantizes MXFP4 weights as they are loaded and uses FP8 Tensor Cores for computation, enabling efficient W4A8-MXFP4 execution on Hopper. The right column above keeps DeepGEMM W8A8 as the baseline. At small and medium batch sizes, Humming's W4A8 reaches approximately 4.2× baseline performance on H20 and 4.5× on H200, also substantially outperforming Humming's W8A8 results in the same figure. Reduced weight traffic translates into lower GEMM latency. FlashInfer CUTLASS W4A8 is also an implementation based on Humming's approach, while Humming's current implementation achieves better performance in the benchmarks shown here.
Blackwell adds native Tensor Core support for microscaling formats such as MXFP8 and MXFP4. From datacenter SM100/SM103 devices to SM120/SM121 devices for workstations and personal computing, Humming uses each architecture's low-precision compute capabilities to support W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4 within one kernel and tuning framework.
On B300 (SM103), Humming demonstrates substantial performance gains across all three MX format combinations. Each panel below uses DeepGEMM Contiguous at the corresponding precision as its baseline. At small and medium batch sizes, W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4 reach approximately 1.25×, 1.6×, and 1.4× baseline performance, respectively, and outperform the corresponding FlashInfer implementations across many workloads. Both Indexed and Grouped paths benefit from native low-precision computation, providing efficient options for different expert layouts.
These gains also extend to SM120 and SM121. In the results below, Humming's MXFP4 × MXFP8 W4A8 and NVFP4 × NVFP4 W4A4 outperform FlashInfer CUTLASS at most tested points. On SM121 at small batch sizes, performance gains reach approximately 19% for W4A8 and 9% for W4A4; on SM120, Humming also leads across most tested sizes. The unified architecture brings these low-precision inference optimizations to more devices, extending efficient quantized computation beyond the datacenter.
End-to-End Inference Performance
Humming's W4A8 gains extend to model serving. In our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash test on eight H20 GPUs with TP=8, keeping the model's MXFP4 weights unchanged and switching MoE execution from Marlin W4A16 (BF16 activations) to Humming W4A8 (tokenwise FP8 activations) improves end-to-end throughput by approximately 14%–43% and reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by approximately 25%–32% . The throughput advantage grows with concurrency: at concurrency 64, output throughput rises from 442.37 to 633.94 tokens/s, while mean time per output token (TPOT) falls by approximately 31% .
Concurrency MoE backend Input throughput (tokens/s) ↑ Output throughput (tokens/s) ↑ TTFT (ms) ↓ TPOT (ms) ↓ 1 vLLM Marlin W4A16 2827.15 88.30 543.13 9.24 1 Humming W4A8 3226.23 (+14.1%) 100.77 (+14.1%) 383.80 (-29.3%) 8.46 (-8.5%) 2 vLLM Marlin W4A16 4781.06 149.33 794.31 10.33 2 Humming W4A8 5646.98 (+18.1%) 176.38 (+18.1%) 555.66 (-30.0%) 9.20 (-10.9%) 4 vLLM Marlin W4A16 7427.64 231.99 1422.32 11.72 4 Humming W4A8 9160.81 (+23.3%) 286.12 (+23.3%) 971.74 (-31.7%) 10.22 (-12.9%) 8 vLLM Marlin W4A16 9190.03 287.04 2049.81 19.90 8 Humming W4A8 12263.89 (+33.4%) 383.04 (+33.4%) 1386.91 (-32.3%) 15.49 (-22.2%) 16 vLLM Marlin W4A16 11124.67 348.96 2463.69 36.28 16 Humming W4A8 15171.00 (+36.4%) 475.89 (+36.4%) 1844.71 (-25.1%) 26.44 (-27.1%) 32 vLLM Marlin W4A16 12669.43 398.83 3546.74 66.44 32 Humming W4A8 17804.79 (+40.5%) 560.49 (+40.5%) 2465.47 (-30.5%) 47.48 (-28.5%) 64 vLLM Marlin W4A16 13937.42 442.37 5467.35 123.25 64 Humming W4A8 19973.00 (+43.3%) 633.94 (+43.3%) 3882.94 (-29.0%) 85.70 (-30.5%)
Usage
Installation
Install Humming with pip:
pip install humming-kernels
Humming uses a CUDA compiler to generate kernels on demand. If no CUDA compiler is available on the system, choose one of the following installation options to include the compilation dependencies for your environment's CUDA major version:
pip install "humming-kernels[cu12]" # CUDA 12 pip install "humming-kernels[cu13]" # CUDA 13
Humming itself is extremely lightweight, with simple dependencies and a wheel package of only about 500 KB. On-demand compilation avoids bundling a large collection of precompiled kernels. In principle, any environment capable of running PyTorch 2.7 can also run Humming, making it easy to integrate into existing inference environments.
Using Humming in vLLM
Humming is deeply integrated into vLLM. Starting with vLLM 0.29.0, CUDA installations include Humming as a dependency, so no separate Humming installation is needed. Humming supports NVIDIA GPUs across all architectures from Turing onward (SM75 and above).
The --linear-backend and --moe-backend options select Humming as the compute backend for dense GEMM and MoE GEMM, respectively. For example, enable Humming for both with tensor parallel size 8:
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --linear-backend humming --moe-backend humming

Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal .
The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more than $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which include deals still in negotiation.
And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers.
Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report.
Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage.
Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion , up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
Tim Fernholz
Kirsten Korosec
1:40 PM PDT · October 20, 2026
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in the third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.
CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing .
That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.
The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.
The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.
During a livestreamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.
“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”
In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12- to 18-month delays in obtaining the metals that blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.
Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.
SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.
Despite those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.
Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”
More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.
This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.

items.title: Google 与 Meta 发布 TorchTPU：PyTorch 原生 TPU 后端
items.title_en: Introducing TorchTPU
items.summary: Google 与 Meta 发布开源项目 TorchTPU，为 Google TPU 提供原生 PyTorch 后端，模型迁移只需把 .to("cuda") 改为 .to("tpu")。
items.fullContent:
Introducing TorchTPU - PyTorch
Close Search
Blog Introducing TorchTPU
By The TorchTPU Team† October 20, 2026 No Comments
Featured projects
TL;DR
TorchTPU is an open source collaboration between Google and Meta that introduces a native and principled PyTorch backend for Google TPUs. It enables seamless out-of-the-box model execution and TPU migration while delivering industry-competitive inference and training performance through eager execution optimizations, torch.compile integration, and native hardware acceleration.
Introducing TorchTPU
Google TPUs have been used very successfully, both within and outside of Google, to train and deploy large ML models at massive scale. They are specifically designed for ML and, as such, they provide significant benefits in terms of performance, energy, and cost. While TPUs have been historically associated with the TensorFlow and the JAX ecosystems, we’re excited to introduce TorchTPU , a new effort started at Google in mid 2025, in collaboration with the PyTorch Team at Meta, to run PyTorch natively on TPUs.
To program Google’s TPU at a level below the Python framework, developers utilize the XLA compiler stack. In 2020, Google introduced the first compiled version of PyTorch for TPU, PyTorch/XLA, based on Lazy Tensors. While foundational, this initial integration struggled to keep pace with the rapid, community-driven evolution of PyTorch. Crucially, PyTorch/XLA required intrusive source-code modifications to explicitly define compilable regions, suffered from severe compile-time latency, lacked support for PyTorch’s native imperative (“eager”) execution mode, and lagged in supporting emerging distributed computing primitives within the PyTorch ecosystem. In contrast with previous efforts such as PyTorch/XLA and TorchAX, which shoehorn PyTorch into JAX’s modus operandi, TorchTPU was built as a principled TPU backend for PyTorch: eager execution is a top priority, and existing PyTorch workloads run out of the box with trivial code changes (e.g., .to("cuda") → .to("tpu") ).
More specifically, as we started TorchTPU we deliberately formulated a set of principles to follow:
PyTorch Citizenship : No JAX dependencies in the runtime;
Solid eager mode;
Torch.compile() based on Torch Dynamo (not Lazy Tensor) and with similar performance to JAX compile;
Wide support for PyTorch distributed idioms (DDP, FSDP, DTensor, …) by providing TPU collectives at the lowest level in the PyTorch stack (e.g. Process Group API);
Seamless integration into the PyTorch ecosystem;
Community engagement.
Focus on the User: Porting a workload to TPU should be as simple as changing model.to("cuda") to model.to("tpu") . (One cannot achieve peak TPU performance with that simple change, since a model’s shapes, sharding and ops may be skewed toward a GPU architecture; however, the model should run out of the box.)
Provide user-friendly and actionable messages for runtime/compiler errors;
Integrate with the tools and frameworks that the PyTorch community already uses (e.g., torch.profiler, DTensor, Ray).
Improve the State of the Art : Build a solution that can compete with PyTorch on GPUs for large scale workloads;
Introduce a JIT compilation approach for eager execution, with runtime optimizations that can bridge the performance gap between op-by-op execution and compiled execution;
Improve the TPU programming stack by introducing bounded dynamism, by avoiding XLA recompilation due to shape changes, and by exploring dynamic TPU kernels that can be precompiled ahead of time.
TorchTPU is in active development, it is used in production for both inference and training workloads for some of the largest Google Cloud customers, and can be found as an Open Source project in this GitHub repo . At the time of this writing, we have:
Added support for both eager and compiled modes, including a new DeferAndFuse eager mode;
Added support for ~450 Aten ops (skipping ops with structural or composite delegates), including forward and backward pass for all Core ATen ops required for the major deep learning architectures;
Added ability to author custom kernels via JAX/Pallas and via Helion DSL;
Validated out-of-box execution on the 5,000 most downloaded Hugging Face models, including: LLMs: Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma, LLama, Mistral, GPT, OPT, BLOOM, Falcon, StableML
Audio/Speech: Whisper, Wav2Vec2, HuBERT, MMS
Vision: DinoV2, SigLIP, CLIP, Swin Transformer, ConvNeXt, ViT, ResNet, DETR
Text Encoders & Search: BERT, ALBERT & Electra, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, T5, MT5, Flan-T5
Validated DTensor-based sharding;
Validated multi-host inference (vLLM and SGLang) and fine-tuning / training workloads (TorchTitan), with Ray-based orchestration;
Validated integration with vLLM, SGLang, TorchTitan, Ray, and TorchRec.
In the remainder of this document we discuss key aspects of the TorchTPU architecture and some initial results.
Architecture Deep Dive
A TPU Primer
Google TPUs are specialized ASICs designed specifically to perform the massive tensor operations that are the foundation of deep learning. From a HW architecture perspective , a TPU chip contains (depending on the generation):
One or more TensorCores , each comprising one or more matrix-multiply units (MXUs), a vector unit (VPU), and a scalar unit (see this link ). Based on the TPU generation, an MXU can include 256×256 multiply-accumulators, which are arranged as a systolic array .
One or more SparseCores , which are specialized units for sparse operations (e.g., gather, scatter, embeddings) and for collectives. They can run in parallel with a TensorCore, enabling compute-compute and compute-communication overlaps.
A large High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) – 288 GB at 8.6 TB/s in TPU 8i , which can be used to store ML data and share that with the CPU.
Bidirectional Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) – 19.2 TBps in TPU 8t and 8i , allowing fast communication between TPU chips within user-configured TPU Slices , which are logical subgroups of a TPU Pod , comprising of a preconfigured number of TPU chips connected in a 3D torus (for TPU 7, TPUv 8t) or Boardfly (TPU 8i) configuration.
Bidirectional Data-Center-Network (DCN) – 400 GBps in TPU 8t , allowing communication between TPU chips across Slices.
TPUs are programmed with the XLA compiler stack through two different entry points: StableHLO (higher-level IR for ML ops) and Mosaic (lower-level IR for custom kernels). The actual TPU ISA is proprietary, subject to change, and not publicly available. Effectively, one can think of StableHLO and (even more so) of Mosaic as equivalent to PTX. See picture below for a high-level sketch.
A C++ program can access a local TPU by instantiating a PjRT Client , whose API provides methods to compile MLIR (StableHLO or Mosaic) into a TPU executable, to launch that executable, and to copy data to-from the TPU. Note that TPU execution is asynchronous and the CPU can wait for a TPU result to be ready by waiting on the associated PjRTBuffer.
Notable features of the TPU programming model:
A TensorCore device can be thought of as a single-threaded processor with one or more massive matrix-multiply units (MXU). Consequently, to reach peak performance it is key that a model’s shapes be sufficiently wide to exploit the full potential of the MXU. This differs from GPUs where launching multiple smaller kernels in parallel can help maximize HW utilization.
The XLA compiler can instruct a TensorCore to offload sparse and collective operations to SparseCore, for more efficient and/or parallel execution. This happens either automatically or through user-supplied MLIR annotation in a compiled StableHLO module.
A TPU device can be accessed by only one user-space process. Following our goal of seamless integration in the PyTorch ecosystem, for distributed TorchTPU workloads we adopt a one-process-per-device model in contrast with JAX’s one-process-per-host model. However, because a TPU can be accessed by only one user-space process, RL colocation can’t be supported out of the box and we are investigating ways to relax or workaround this TPU limitation.
StableHLO follows the SSA paradigm and, hence, doesn’t allow for in-place mutations, i.e., a write operation always produces a new value (at least conceptually). This is particularly significant for TorchTPU, which does provide familiar Pytorch “view” semantics, including mutations, through view decomposition and inversion, as explained later in this doc.
The XLA compiler and PjRT runtime assume that tensor shapes are known at compile time. Recognizing this as a limitation for PyTorch workloads, we have been adding support for bounded dynamism, i.e., when the maximum bounds of a shape’s dimensions are known at compile time, but the actual dimensions are known only at runtime.
Collective ops are lowered to XLA as StableHLO ops, versus using a separate library such as NCCL.
Usability and Autoload Mechanism
We designed TorchTPU with usability in mind. When the user imports PyTorch on a TPU machine where TorchTPU wheel is installed, running the PyTorch code on TPU involves only trivial changes and can be done in a couple of lines of code thanks to PyTorch’s autoload mechanism:
See the table below for a side-by-side comparison.
Before (GPU) After (TPU) Alternative (TPU or GPU) import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
def main():
device = torch.device("cuda")
dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")
rank = dist.get_rank()
word_size = dist.get_world_size()
...
model = model.to(device)
... import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
def main():
device = torch.device("tpu")
dist.init_process_group(backend="tpu_dist")
rank = dist.get_rank()
word_size = dist.get_world_size()
...
model = model.to(device)
... import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
def main():
device = torch.accelerator.current_accelerator()
dist.init_process_group()
rank = dist.get_rank()
word_size = dist.get_world_size()

Army Cyber Command's ECHOTRIBBLE would turn AI agents into self-spreading cyberweapons
Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner
Oct 20, 2026
Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER
Internal documents show the Army Cyber Command is building AI agents that move through other networks on their own and "neutralize" targets. Experts warn the collateral damage would be nearly impossible to control.
The Army Cyber Command (ARCYBER) is developing a platform meant to turn AI agents into autonomous weapons, according to documents obtained by The Intercept . A paper for potential contractors says the program, codenamed "ECHOTRIBBLE," is "designed to autonomously navigate infrastructures." It's supposed to be capable of "identifying and neutralizing identified threats/targets."
Right now, soldiers at computers carry out most of ARCYBER's offensive hacking operations. A Q&A document for interested vendors makes clear that ECHOTRIBBLE is "primarily focused" on attacks. According to the document, neutralizing a target could mean "disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target."
The system is supposed to work like a computer worm, jumping undetected from device to device until it finds its target. That's meant to work in the cloud as well as on "air-gapped" systems with no network connection. Once the job is done, the agents are supposed to destroy themselves. The Army can set "predefined triggers" at the start, but the software "must operate with minimal human oversight" and be capable of "Self-Directed Behavior."
The Intercept reports that the program is still in its early stages. A presentation for potential vendors at an ARCYBER event on June 24 showed what it could look like. Once the software lands on a laptop, it "identifies other potential targets" on the same network and "produces a replica of itself tailored specifically for the iPad, Apple desktop, and Windows 11 PC."
An ARCYBER slide shows how ECHOTRIBBLE could spread through a network. | Image: ARCYBER ECHOTRIBBLE would turn AI lab accidents into a weapon
Over the past few months, agents in tests by OpenAI and other companies have repeatedly broken into outside systems and their developers' own systems without meaning to. Targets included RubyGems , Hugging Face , and the Australian government's Medicare statistics portal . Agents also tried to break into the US Department of Education. In none of these cases had they been told to attack.
AI systems have been seen knowingly attacking systems that weren't even their targets, says David Krueger, a machine learning professor at the University of Montreal. Given these known failure patterns, ordering autonomous systems to "neutralize" threats is "incredibly dangerous," he says.
Hyrum Anderson, CEO of AI security firm Abundant, also warns about damage on the way to the target. An agent could hit a US water utility, for example, if an adversary has set up its command infrastructure there. Organizations below a "security poverty line," from dental offices to critical infrastructure, face the most risk, he says. Under pressure, agents often treat guardrails as obstacles, and once the order is "destroy," the blast radius could grow dramatically.
William Marcellino of the RAND Corporation points to the systems' lack of judgment. People trust a 19-year-old Marine with live ammunition because he knows enough about the world to recognize what he shouldn't do, he says. Today's publicly available AI doesn't have that ability.

items.title: llm-d 1.0 发布：Kubernetes 原生分布式推理服务走向生产就绪
items.title_en: llm-d 1.0 hardens open-source AI inference for production
items.summary: IBM、Red Hat 和 Google 等主导的开源推理项目 llm-d 在 PyTorch Conference North America 上发布 llm-d 1.0，这是一个 Kubernetes 原生的分布式推理服务框架，支持任意模型、任意加速器和任意云。
items.fullContent:
llm-d 1.0 hardens open-source AI inference for production - IBM Research
Today at the PyTorch Conference North America, llm-d project contributors are announcing llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for open-source AI infrastructure. A Kubernetes-native distributed inference serving network , llm-d makes it possible to deploy inference stacks for any model, on any accelerator, in any cloud.
The release signals that llm-d has moved beyond demonstrating individual performance techniques and is ready to support the realities of production: sustained efficiency under many workloads, all while balancing service priorities amid growing demand. And with inference costs increasing, llm-d is meant to help bring model deployment in-house and deliver returns on AI investment.
The work has been developed with a growing open-source community that includes hardware providers, model developers, cloud platforms, and enterprise users. As lead maintainers of llm-d, Red Hat, IBM, and Google have helped turn advanced inference techniques into a coordinated system that enterprises can operate at scale. The three co-founded llm-d last year with CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and industry leaders including AMD, Cisco, Hugging Face, Intel, Lambda, and Mistral AI have joined as contributors along the way.
The result is a vendor-neutral alternative for organizations that want frontier-class inference performance without depending entirely on one proprietary model provider, cloud, or hardware platform.
“llm-d is ready for day 2 operations,” said Carlos Costa, Distinguished Engineer at IBM Research, llm-d co-founder and lead maintainer. “llm-d has been delivering state-of-the-art inference performance for production workloads. What 1.0 adds is the maturity to run it like any other critical service: a stable API, multiple tenants with competing priorities sharing the same infrastructure, and upgrades that don't interrupt operations. That is what we built llm-d 1.0 to do.”
A full production stack
Since llm-d launched, the project has focused on five important approaches to improving AI inference: prefix-cache-aware routing, which directs a request to infrastructure that may already hold its shared context; KV-cache offloading, which expands the useful life of cached information by moving it across GPU, CPU, and storage resources; batch inference optimization, which groups work so infrastructure can process it more efficiently; prefill/decode disaggregation, which separates the work of reading a prompt from the work of generating a response; and wide expert parallelism, which distributes large mixture-of-experts models across many accelerators.
These ideas are not new to version 1.0. What is new is the level of integration and operational maturity around them.
With version 1.0, llm-d has matured into a stack capable of supporting day 2 operations: everything that must happen after an AI service is deployed. That includes serving workloads with competing priorities, managing different performance requirements, maintaining efficiency, prioritizing important services, and keeping the system dependable over time. A benchmark can show that one feature improves throughput, but a production system must keep delivering that performance when traffic changes, hardware fails, software is updated, or different users compete for the same resources. llm-d 1.0 is about making the individual techniques work together under those less predictable conditions.
One endpoint, different kinds of work
Expanding on the core technical innovations that have already made llm-d a powerful tool for distributed inference, llm-d 1.0 enhances support for multi-tenant quality of service, zero-downtime operations, and agent-aware serving, for sustained performance in common day 2 production operations. An enterprise AI service may receive requests from people and autonomous agents through the same endpoint, but those workloads behave differently. A person using a coding assistant expects a fast answer. An agent may send a large burst of requests, pause while using a tool, and then return for another round of model calls.
With flow control , llm-d 1.0 manages competing priorities whether workloads share the same hardware or span a mix of accelerators. Flow control, fairness, and prioritization help prevent bursty workloads from overwhelming latency-sensitive services. Under heavy demand, the system can make more deliberate decisions about which requests should receive resources first. Requests can also remain pinned to the appropriate infrastructure across multiple turns. That keeps their prefix caches warm, increasing the chance that previously processed context can be reused instead of calculated again.
This matters for conversational assistants, but it is especially valuable for agents. Agents frequently return to the same code, documents, instructions, and conversation history while carrying out a task. Prefix-cache-aware routing sends each turn toward a replica that already holds the relevant context, while KV-cache offloading helps preserve more of that reusable information when GPU memory becomes constrained. This is what production readiness looks like in practice: serving a model more effectively and more cost-effectively by understanding the work arriving at that model and managing infrastructure accordingly.
Improving AI ROI with better infrastructure
This production focus leads directly to the economics of AI. As AI moves into everyday business operations, inference has become a recurring expense. Agentic systems can increase that expense because a single assignment may involve many rounds of reasoning, tool use, evaluation, and revision. If every step requires a model to reread the same material, you’re repeatedly paying for work the system has already done.
In a recent test of an agentic coding workload, llm-d’s prefix-aware router captured 97% of the available cache reuse . By avoiding repeated computation and making more efficient use of existing hardware, techniques like this can reduce the cost of serving AI at scale. In another recent demonstration, IBM and Red Hat ran 3,000 software-engineering agents concurrently on a self-hosted deployment for 5 to 10 times less than the actual price of serving the same open model as a service.
When an organization operates its own infrastructure, the infrastructure becomes part of a cost structure that can be managed. By combining open-weight models with an open serving stack, llm-d gives organizations another option for controlling the relationship between AI consumption, infrastructure spending, and business value.
Connecting the open-source AI Ecosystem
llm-d works with inference engines such as vLLM or SGLang , adding the distributed routing and operational capabilities needed to turn model servers into production services.
That also gives llm-d an important role in the broader open-source ecosystem. PyTorch is closely associated with the people developing AI models and applications. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), which hosts llm-d as a sandbox project, focuses more heavily on deploying and operating systems in production. The llm-d project is a bridge between these worlds.
“llm-d unifies the PyTorch and CNCF ecosystems by bringing Kubernetes-native orchestration directly to vLLM and modern inference engines,” said Stephen Watt, vice president, office of the chief technology officer, Red Hat. “It delivers high-performance, distributed inference with the reliability and scale enterprises need — all within an operational model they already know.”
IBM’s contribution to llm-d reflects a long-standing approach: Take ideas that can improve computing and turn them into open technologies that organizations can use in the real world.
With llm-d 1.0, that work has helped produce an inference stack designed not only to perform well, but to keep performing when AI becomes critical infrastructure. Open-source AI inference is ready to be operated, governed, and optimized in production.

items.fullContent:
¡Llegamos a Madrid! Waymo is coming to Spain
Waypoint: The official Waymo blog
Today, we are excited to announce that Waymo is laying the groundwork for our fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Spain, beginning with the Region of Madrid. With over 20 million trips completed and hundreds of thousands of commercial rides served each week, we are excited to be a part of the region’s transportation ecosystem. We aim to welcome our first riders in 2027.
In the coming days, you’ll begin to see Waymo’s electric Jaguar I-PACE vehicles on the streets of the region. We are taking a methodical, phased, safety-first approach that begins with manual driving before progressing to rigorous technical validation with local, trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel. This validation period will ensure the Waymo Driver adapts seamlessly to the region’s unique traffic patterns and road conditions.
“Madrid is an incredible capital of innovation and an integral part of our growing global presence. We can’t wait to serve Madrileños,” said Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana. “We’re proud to bring Waymo to Spain, beginning with the Region of Madrid. We share the region’s commitment to safer, more accessible, and zero-emission mobility, and we look forward to serving as a collaborative partner in achieving those goals.”
Spain has a long-standing commitment to road safety and modern mobility, values that align directly with our safety-first approach. We are actively engaging with national, regional, and local authorities, and familiarising emergency services with our technology as we look to safely serve riders in the future. We are also engaging with local partners and are investing in the local operations needed to support our service. We look forward to building a collaborative presence that aligns with Spanish national and regional regulatory frameworks and community needs.
“Technology reaches its true purpose when placed at the service of people. At FESVIAL, we believe autonomous driving represents a great opportunity to turn innovation into an ally of human capability and road safety, helping prevent mistakes, anticipate risks, and save lives,” said Ignacio Lijarcio, President of the Spanish Road Safety Foundation. “The arrival of new autonomous mobility solutions in Spain should allow us to move forward, with rigor and confidence, toward a mobility model that is increasingly safe, accessible, and centered on people."
The Waymo Driver is designed to strengthen urban mobility, while supporting the region's vision for safer and more accessible mobility. The data from over 400 million fully autonomous kilometres driven shows the Waymo Driver was involved in 95% fewer (20x fewer) crashes involving serious injury or worse compared to humans in the cities where we operate.
“Autonomous vehicles represent a major step forward in reducing traffic casualties by eliminating human error, which is behind more than 90% of road accidents. Their technology removes the main driver risks: distractions, fatigue, alcohol and drug consumption, speeding, or failing to maintain safe following distances,” said Mar Cogollos, Director for the Spanish Association for the Study of Spinal Cord Injury. “For AESLEME, the priority is to achieve safe mobility where no one loses their life or suffers serious injury in an avoidable road accident.”
We look forward to embarking on this journey with the Region of Madrid. Head to waymo.com/waymo-in-spain to sign up for updates and follow our progress.
Hoy nos complace anunciar que estamos sentando las bases para desplegar nuestro servicio de transporte de viajeros en vehículos totalmente autónomos en España, comenzando por la Comunidad de Madrid. Con más de 20 millones de viajes completados y cientos de miles de trayectos comerciales realizados cada semana, nos entusiasma formar parte del ecosistema de transporte de la región. Nuestro objetivo es dar la bienvenida a nuestros primeros usuarios en 2027.
En los próximos días, comenzarás a ver los vehículos eléctricos Jaguar I-PACE de Waymo por las calles de la región. Adoptaremos un enfoque metódico, por fases y donde la seguridad es lo primero, que comenzará con la conducción manual antes de avanzar hacia una rigurosa validación técnica con especialistas en vehículos autónomos locales y capacitados al volante. Este periodo de validación garantizará que Waymo Driver se adapte sin problemas a los patrones de tráfico y a las condiciones viales específicas de la Comunidad.
"Madrid es una increíble capital de la innovación y una parte integral de nuestra creciente presencia global. Estamos deseando dar servicio a los madrileños", afirmó la codirectora ejecutiva de Waymo, Tekedra Mawakana. "Nos enorgullece traer Waymo a España, comenzando por la Comunidad de Madrid. Compartimos el compromiso de la región con una movilidad más segura, más accesible y de cero emisiones, y esperamos trabajar como socios colaboradores para alcanzar esos objetivos".
España cuenta con un compromiso histórico con la seguridad vial y la movilidad moderna, valores que se alinean directamente con nuestro enfoque centrado en la seguridad. Estamos colaborando activamente con las autoridades nacionales, autonómicas y locales a lo largo de nuestras operaciones, y ayudaremos a los servicios de emergencia a familiarizarse con nuestra tecnología mientras nos preparamos para prestar servicio a los usuarios en el futuro. Asimismo, nos estamos vinculando con socios locales  e invirtiendo en las operaciones locales necesarias para respaldar nuestro servicio. Esperamos continuar y profundizar en estas alianzas para garantizar que nuestra actividad se alinea a la perfección con los marcos regulatorios de España y de la región, así como con las necesidades locales.
“La tecnología alcanza su verdadero propósito cuando se pone al servicio de las personas. Desde FESVIAL, creemos que la conducción autónoma representa una gran oportunidad para convertir la innovación en una aliada de la capacidad humana y de la seguridad vial, ayudando a prevenir errores, anticipar riesgos y salvar vidas”, sostiene Ignacio Lijarcio, presidente de la Fundación Española para la Seguridad Vial. “La llegada de nuevas soluciones de movilidad autónoma a España debería permitirnos avanzar, con rigor y confianza, hacia un modelo de movilidad cada vez más seguro, accesible y centrado en las personas”.
Waymo Driver está diseñado para reforzar la movilidad urbana, apoyando al mismo tiempo la visión de la región de conseguir una movilidad más segura y accesible. Los datos tras recorrer más de 400 millones de kilómetros de forma totalmente autónoma con pasajeros demuestran que Waymo Driver ha registrado un 95% menos de accidentes con lesiones graves o mortales que los conductores humanos en las ciudades donde opera, lo que equivale a una tasa de siniestralidad 20 veces inferior.
“Los vehículos autónomos representan un avance crucial en la reducción de las víctimas de tráfico al eliminar el error humano, que está detrás de más del 90% de los accidentes de carretera. Su tecnología elimina los principales riesgos relacionados con la conducción: distracciones, fatiga, consumo de alcohol y drogas, exceso de velocidad o el incumplimiento de la distancia de seguridad”, declara Mar Cogollos, directora de la Asociación Española para el Estudio de la Lesión Medular. “Para AESLEME, la prioridad es lograr una movilidad segura donde nadie pierda la vida ni sufra lesiones graves en un accidente de tráfico evitable”.
Esperamos con ilusión emprender este viaje junto a la Comunidad de Madrid. Para más información y registrarte para recibir novedades, visita waymo.com/waymo-in-spain .

items.title: Databricks 发布 MemCurrent 生产级 Agent 持久记忆架构
items.title_en: MemCurrent: Designing Persistent Memory for Production Agents
items.summary: Databricks 介绍 MemCurrent，一种面向生产 Agent 的持久记忆架构，结合情景记忆与派生记忆，通过插件、工具调用和离线 dreaming 管线三种访问模式读写与整合记忆，已用于 Agent Bricks Memory 和 Genie。
items.fullContent:
MemCurrent: Designing Persistent Memory for Production Agents | Databricks Blog Skip to main content
AI tools have made it easy to vibe code agents. Building and maintaining an enterprise agent in production, however, remains significantly more challenging. In particular, developers are often forced to make a trade-off between quality (getting good answers, especially on long-tail tasks) and efficiency (keeping cost and latency in check at scale). Oftentimes, techniques bring gains in one dimension at the cost of another.
Memory is a promising way to improve both at the same time. It can help agents carry useful context across tasks, such as user preferences, prior corrections, metric definitions, and successful workflows. In principle, this can improve accuracy, reduce repeated errors, and avoid unnecessary rediscovery. But more history is not necessarily better memory. Supplying every past interaction is costly and can introduce stale, conflicting, or irrelevant context. The central challenge is deciding what to retain, how to maintain it, and how to measure usefulness.
In this post, we introduce MemCurrent , a persistent memory architecture for production agents, which now powers the new Agent Bricks Memory and Genie . Agents read and write memory as they work, and an offline “dreaming” pipeline consolidates memory to keep it consistent and fresh. On our internal benchmark, built from realistic enterprise tasks, MemCurrent triples the agent's pass rate over having no memory, while using 31% fewer tokens and running 26% faster. The rest of this post covers how we designed and evaluated it, and what we learned along the way.
Figure 1. Pass rate vs. tokens per task on our Internal Memory Benchmark. MemCurrent is on the Pareto frontier, outperforming Mem0, PropMem, and OpenClaw memory on both dimensions.
How We Designed Memory
There are three ways to wire memory into an agent. As a plugin (like our earlier work on MemAlign and Memory Scaling ), memory is read and written automatically at fixed points in a session. As tools , the agent decides what and when to read and write. As an offline pipeline , memory is updated in the background on a schedule or trigger, and used in later sessions. Each comes with trade-offs:

Agent
Online
Updates take effect immediately
Agent has flexibility
Higher runtime cost and latency
Quality constrained by agent capability
Pipeline Schedule or trigger Offline Lower runtime cost and latency (async batched)
Updates arrive with a delay
Table 1. Three access patterns of memory: plugin, tool, or offline pipeline.
MemCurrent uses all three, each where it fits best.
Figure 2. Overview of MemCurrent.
MemCurrent has two types of memory: episodic memory , which stores raw session traces; and derived memory , which has the distilled learnings from these traces, stored as files in a structured knowledge base. An auto-generated memory.md index sits at the top, describing the file structure and what each file contains.
Both episodic and derived memory live in a production-grade database that can scale to many users while delivering low-latency responses. Episodic memory is append-only, where a plugin logs each step as the session runs. Derived memory is a mutable table simulating a hierarchical file system, where writing happens in two ways. Agent tools ( add_memory, update_memory, delete_memory ) handle explicit requests like “Never write scripts in the /tmp dir”. An offline dreaming pipeline captures the rest, distilling implicit learnings from each new session into the relevant files. It also cleans up the whole store, splitting oversized files, merging duplicates, and resolving conflicts.
Reading works in layers. At session start, a plugin injects the memory index, so the agent knows what it knows before it begins. During the session, the agent has two tools that work across both memory types: search_memory returns the top matches for a query (a step in a past trace, or a line in a memory file), and fetch_memory returns the full entry by identifier (session ID or file path).
How We Evaluated Memory
Benchmarks
We start with three popular open-source benchmarks: LoCoMo , LongMemEval , and ConvoMem . All three test whether an agent can recall facts stated earlier in open-ended synthetic conversations.
In addition, we built an Internal Memory Benchmark from real Genie conversations, where users ask all kinds of questions about their data. As in Figure 3, we started from 12K+ sessions, mined 3K candidates containing memory-worthy signals, and drafted a follow-up question with scoring rubrics. The other sessions from the same user serve as fillers for the test case. An adversarial judge then checked each test case against 7 criteria, such as whether the knowledge is actually present, specific to the user, required to answer, natural, and verifiable. After a final manual review, the benchmark has a total of 114 test cases, with 29 users and 2,233 history sessions.
Figure 3. How we built our Internal Memory Benchmark.
Here's an example:
Figure 4. An example test case from our Internal Memory Benchmark. In a past session, the user corrects the agent's choice of table and tells it to exclude background requests. Later, the agent faces a different but related question, and has to find that session among 100+ others and apply what it learned. The output is scored by an LLM judge based on a list of rubrics (some memory-dependent, some task-intrinsic).
Our benchmark differs from existing ones in three ways:
Enterprise domain. Existing benchmarks are open-ended chats about the lives of simulated personas. Ours is from real work in a data workspace, involving rich enterprise knowledge like table semantics, metric definitions, and workflows.
Memory feeds actions, not answers. Finding the right string in past conversations is not enough; agents must apply retrieved knowledge to complete multi-step tasks.
Diversity. Test cases span 5 memory types (profile, preferences, domain knowledge, projects, workflows) crossed with 11 scenarios (direct instruction, changing or outdated facts, multi-session aggregation, memory-independent questions, and more).
Results
We compare MemCurrent with three open-source memory backends, Mem0 , PropMem , OpenClaw memory , using the same underlying LLM.
Open-Source Benchmarks. We pair each memory backend with a simple question-answering agent, built with two agent harnesses (LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK). We also run two baselines: a floor with no memory , and a ceiling with full context , where every past session goes into the agent's context. Across all three benchmarks, MemCurrent scores highest among all memory backends and stays on the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier . On average, MemCurrent (88.1%) performs on par with full context (87.8%) at ~12x fewer input tokens per question (8.4K vs 103K). On the two benchmarks with the longest histories, it even beats full context, where dumping everything into the prompt ends up confusing the agent.
Figure 5. Cost–accuracy 1 trade-off of memory backends on (a) LoCoMo (19–32 sessions/sample), (b) LongMemEval (s split) (38–62 sessions/sample), and (c) ConvoMem (stratified subset of 500 samples, 100 sessions/sample). We use GPT 5.6 luna as the agent and memory model. All memory backends are run as a plugin, which automatically searches for related memories to the question and injects them into the agent context at session start. 2 Accuracy is the mean over the LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK harnesses and 3 repeats. Cost is mean input tokens per question (log scale).
Internal Memory Benchmark. On our benchmark, the gap widens. Here, each memory backend runs inside our internal Genie, the same agent the benchmark sessions came from. The histories are too long to fit in context, so our ceiling is gold injection: injecting only the gold memories into the agent's context. Among all memory backends, MemCurrent has the highest pass rate (68.4%) and the lowest latency (252s) and token usage (418K), closing over 80% of the gap between no memory (22.3%) and gold injection (78.6%). Notably, while Mem0 was also on frontier on earlier benchmarks, it trails at 43.9% here with higher latency and cost. Compared to no memory, MemCurrent triples the agent's pass rate (22.3% → 68.4%) while making it 1.35x faster and 1.44x cheaper .
Figure 6. Pass rate, mean latency, and mean token usage per task on our Internal Memory Benchmark across 3 repeats. We use Claude Opus 4.6 as the agent model and GPT 5.6 sol as the memory model. All memory backends are provided as agent tools and a session-start plugin.
MemCurrent in Action
In addition to benchmark numbers, let's examine two examples of how MemCurrent helps in practice, from internal Genie sessions.
Example 1: Memory stops an occasional hallucination mistake. In Figure 7, a user asked the agent for the top 20 users of Product X over the past two months. The agent wrote a correct SQL query, but never read the actual execution results saved to a file. It still confidently produced a table with hallucinated content. Upon user feedback, the agent saved the lesson to memory. Next time, once the query ran, the agent read the results first and returned the right table. One memory correction kept a one-off slip from becoming a habit.
Figure 7. An anonymized example of how memory helps the agent avoid a repeated hallucination mistake.
Example 2: Memory saves computation on related tasks. In Figure 8, a user asked for “the top 5 SDP customers”. The agent had to figure everything out from scratch: what “SDP” stands for, which tables held usage data, and how to join and filter them. It took 11 tool calls, 8 subagents, and nearly six minutes. The agent saved these steps as a workflow file in memory, which it could reuse on related tasks. Later, the user asked a different question: how many SDP customers had more than 5K pipeline runs last month. Using the workflow, the agent answered with 2 tool calls and 1 subagent in 41 seconds. The question was new, but the path to the answer wasn't, and memory let the agent skip unnecessary exploration.
Figure 8. An anonymized example of how memory turns a 6 minute task into 41 seconds.
What Makes MemCurrent Work
To understand what accounts for MemCurrent's superior performance, we ran ablations on our Internal Memory Benchmark for two design choices: memory types and extraction strategy.
Do we need both memory types? Episodic memory alone helps moderately: 35.8%, up from 22.3% with no memory. The raw history is useful, but the agent only searches it in about a third of test cases, though it passes 60% of those when it does. Derived memory avoids this issue, as the injected memory index at session start gives the agent information about what's available in memory and when to look, lifting pass rate to 66.1%. Adding episodic memory on top gives the best result, at 68.4%. The gain is small, but it suggests raw traces can recover details that distillation drops.
Figure 9. Pass rate by memory type.
What's a good memory extraction strategy? As shown in Figure 2, two channels extract derived memory: online tools and offline dreaming. When isolated, offline dreaming (63.5%) beats online tools (53.9%) by nearly 10 points. Their combination produces the highest pass rate at 66.1%. That supports a split of duties: dreaming handles background extraction and consolidation, while online tools make explicit requests take effect right away.
Figure 10. Pass rate by extraction strategy.
Conclusion
Memory is how an agent stops starting from zero. In this post, we introduced MemCurrent, a memory architecture for production agents that combines episodic memory and derived memory, with three access patterns: plugins to log and load context automatically, tools the agent calls on demand, and an offline dreaming pipeline that consolidates memory in the background.
Across all benchmarks we ran, MemCurrent improves quality and efficiency at the same time, the trade-off we set out to break. On open-source benchmarks, it matches full context performance at about 12x fewer input tokens. On our Internal Memory Benchmark, built from real data work, it triples the agent's pass rate over no memory while also making it faster and cheaper.
The ablations point to where the value comes from. Derived memory does most of the work, and episodic memory adds a smaller boost by recovering details that distillation drops. Combining online tools with offline dreaming makes the best extraction strategy: explicit requests take effect immediately, while dreaming distills implicit learnings and consolidates the store in the background.
Beyond the numbers, memory provides a knowledge base that isn't tied to a single agent or LLM. It can move with users to new agents or LLMs, and could seed knowledge shared across their organization, a direction we are exploring next.
Getting Started
We're bringing these findings to drive improvements across Databricks products:
For agent developers. Agent Bricks is Databricks' developer platform for building custom agents. MemCurrent is built into Agent Bricks' Memory offering, powered by Lakebase. The offering includes:
Session store for episodic memory
Memory store for derived memory
An automatic dreaming pipeline
Tracing and evaluation of agent quality, including the impact of memory
A CLI which helps you quickly get started with an end-to-end sample agent with all of the above in <10 minutes
Get started building your custom agent today.
For Databricks Genie users. Genie is an interface where Databricks users can converse with their data in natural language. MemCurrent is already in action behind the scenes, helping to improve answer quality while reducing response latency and cost.
Get started with Genie.
Authors: Veronica Lyu, Wenhao Zhan, Sam Havens, Ziyi Yang, Jenny Sun, Qinxin Wang, Nihit Desai, Sirui Sun, Ankit Mathur, Jane Zhang, Yi Liu, Jialu Liu, Michael Bendersky, Matei Zaharia, Xing Chen
