items.title: n8n 教程：在 NVIDIA DGX Spark 上离线运行全套 AI 工作流
items.title_en: Run your n8n AI workflows on NVIDIA DGX Spark, with no cloud API
items.summary: n8n 博客发布教程，讲解如何在一台 NVIDIA DGX Spark（128GB 统一内存）上部署七个本地模型，通过 LiteLLM 单一 OpenAI 兼容端点驱动 n8n 工作流，全程不调用云 API。
items.fullContent:
Run your n8n AI workflows on NVIDIA DGX Spark, with no cloud API – n8n Blog
Github ★ 207k Sign in Get Started
Most small businesses want the same handful of AI jobs. They want to draft emails, summarize calls, read invoices, search their own documents, and make the odd image. Plenty of them can't send customer data to a cloud API to do it.
Often the reason is data privacy and sovereignty. A clinic, a law firm, or an accountant may hold records that a contract, a regulator, or a professional duty says must stay under their control. Once that data goes to a cloud API, it sits on someone else's hardware, possibly in another jurisdiction, under terms the provider can change. Running the models on hardware you own keeps the data in your building, and lets you show an auditor exactly where it went.
Your n8n workflows can transcribe calls, read invoices, answer questions from your own documents, and draft replies without sending a byte to a cloud API. This post shows you how to serve every model those workflows need from one NVIDIA DGX Spark, behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint that n8n's OpenAI nodes already speak.
A DGX Spark has 128GB of unified memory shared by the CPU and GPU. That's enough to keep every one of those jobs loaded at once, if you pick the right models. Most of this post is about that.
The self-hosted AI starter kit gets one person running local models on a laptop. This is the next step: a box in the office that serves a whole team, with a model for each job and the code to run it.
In this post, you'll:
Choose models that run fast on the DGX Spark's memory bandwidth
Serve a 35B mixture-of-experts model with vLLM in NVFP4
Fit a full AI stack into one box's shared memory
Route every job through one LiteLLM endpoint with per-team keys
Connect n8n to the stack and build a workflow that never calls a cloud API
Measure what happens to chat speed when someone generates an image
Pick models for the bandwidth, not the parameter count
The DGX Spark's GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip reads memory at 273 GB/s. When a model generates text, it reads its active weights from memory for each token, so the fewer bytes it reads, the faster it runs.
A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model only activates a few experts per token. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B has 35B parameters in total but about 3B active. Stored in NVFP4 (NVIDIA's 4-bit floating point format), those active weights are a small fraction of a dense model's.
On my DGX Spark, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B generated 120 tokens per second for one user, and 359 tokens per second in total across eight users. Those numbers include the reasoning tokens the model writes before it answers.
That gives the first design rule: one strong MoE model for everything text-shaped. Summarizing, classifying, extracting, drafting, coding, and reading screenshots all go to the same model. Every extra model is another container to pin, patch, and monitor, so a specialist model only gets a slot where an LLM can't do the job.
The stack
These are the models that stay loaded on one DGX Spark:
Job Model License Chat, coding, vision, extraction nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 Apache 2.0 Embeddings Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B Apache 2.0 Reranking Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B Apache 2.0 Speech to text openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo MIT Document OCR zai-org/GLM-OCR MIT Image generation Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo Apache 2.0 Text to speech hexgrad/Kokoro-82M Apache 2.0 Every model in the stack allows commercial use. That rule cost more than any technical one, and there's a section on it later.
Step 1: Cache everything for offline use
The stack has to run with the network cable unplugged, so download every model once and record the exact commit you got. This loop caches each model and writes a lock file of repository and commit:
pipx install "huggingface_hub[cli]"
hf auth login
for repo in nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B \
openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo zai-org/GLM-OCR Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo; do
hf download "$repo"
echo "$repo $(cat ~/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--${repo//\//--}/refs/main)" >> models.lock
done When you start a model, pass --revision with the commit from models.lock . vLLM then serves the weights you tested rather than whatever main points to today, so an upstream change can't swap the weights or the license under you.
Check the vLLM version, not the tag
Pin containers the same way, and check what's inside them. My first attempt used vLLM's cu130-nightly tag. That tag had stopped updating, and the image it pulled was five months old, with vLLM 0.19. It couldn't load Qwen3.6 at all. The errors didn't mention versions. They were a KeyError for a missing weight-scale parameter, which reads like a broken checkpoint.
Before you trust an image, print the vLLM version inside it:
docker run --rm --entrypoint python3 <image> -c "import vllm; print(vllm.__version__)" The image that worked was the official vllm/vllm-omni:v0.30.0 , which ships vLLM 0.30.0 with an arm64 build. vLLM-Omni is a full vLLM with extra serving modes for images and speech, so it also serves plain LLMs. Its default entrypoint isn't vllm serve , so wrap it once:
printf 'FROM vllm/vllm-omni:v0.30.0\nENTRYPOINT ["vllm", "serve"]\n' | docker build -t vllm-spark:omni-0.30.0 - The Kokoro-FastAPI image needed a community fix to build on arm64. The Dockerfile comes from a post by swann.schilling on the NVIDIA Developer Forums .
Step 2: Serve the backbone
This command starts the main model in vLLM:
docker run -d --name qwen3.6 --gpus all --ipc=host \
-p 172.17.0.1:8001:8000 \
-e HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 -e VLLM_API_KEY=<your-backend-key> \
-v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
vllm-spark:omni-0.30.0 \
nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 --revision <commit-from-models.lock> \
--served-model-name qwen3.6-35b \
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.32 --max-model-len 65536 \
--max-num-seqs 8 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
--trust-remote-code --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --moe-backend marlin \
--enable-chunked-prefill --async-scheduling --enable-prefix-caching \
--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3,"moe_backend":"triton"}' \
--reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 On my DGX Spark, this model was ready to serve 311 seconds after docker run .
The port is published on 172.17.0.1 , Docker's bridge address, so only containers on this machine can reach it. VLLM_API_KEY makes vLLM reject any request without the key.
The flags that matter most on a DGX Spark:
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.32 caps this model at about a third of memory. The other models need the rest.
--kv-cache-dtype fp8 halves the memory the KV cache needs, so the same budget holds more context.
--moe-backend marlin picks the kernel for the quantized expert layers. The draft model's experts aren't quantized, so --speculative-config sets its own moe_backend .
--speculative-config turns on multi-token prediction (MTP). The model drafts three tokens ahead and checks them in one pass.
--reasoning-parser and --tool-call-parser must match the model family. When tool calling fails, check these flags before you blame the model.
Check the startup log for the kernels vLLM chose. These lines are from my run:
Using MarlinNvFp4LinearKernel for NVFP4 GEMM
Using 'MARLIN' NvFp4 MoE backend out of potential backends: ['FLASHINFER_TRTLLM', 'FLASHINFER_CUTEDSL', ...]
Your GPU does not have native support for FP4 computation but FP4 quantization is being used.
Weight-only FP4 compression will be used leveraging the Marlin kernel. That last warning matters for how you read "NVFP4" on a DGX Spark. With this vLLM build, the weights are stored in 4 bits, but the math runs in 16 bits. You still get most of the benefit, because generating tokens is limited by reading weights from memory, and 4-bit weights are a quarter of the size. Faster FP4 kernels for GB10 may raise these numbers in later builds.
Step 3: Fit the rest into shared memory
On a DGX Spark, the GPU and the operating system share one 128GB pool. Linux reported 121GB of it as total memory on my box. That changes two things you might take for granted on a discrete GPU.
First, --gpu-memory-utilization is a fraction of the whole pool, taken at startup. It's not a fraction of what's free. An instance without a cap tries to take almost everything, and the next model fails to start.
Second, vLLM sizes its cache from the memory that's free when it starts. Start two models at once and they fight over the same memory. Start one at a time, and wait for each to answer its health check before starting the next:
until curl -sf http://172.17.0.1:8001/health; do sleep 5; done If a model fails with CUDA error: out of memory while free shows plenty available, the Linux page cache is holding it. This is common straight after downloading 220GB of weights. Drop the cache, then start the model again:
sudo sh -c 'sync; echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches' This is how long each service took to load from cold, with the page cache dropped first, and how much memory it took:
Service Seconds to ready GB taken qwen3.6 237 43 rerank 106 8 whisper 136 8 ocr 137 11 image 96 20 tts 21 3 The embedding model needed one more flag on vLLM 0.30.0, --convert embed , and started later, after the rest. With all seven models loaded, the DGX Spark used 108GB and had 13GB available. That's the limit of what one DGX Spark holds. Start the stack well before anyone needs it: the six services in the table took about 12 minutes.
vLLM can also fail at startup with Error in memory profiling , when another process frees memory while vLLM measures what's available. On shared memory, that happens if another model is loading or shutting down. Start the model again once the box is quiet.
Step 4: Put one endpoint in front
LiteLLM gives every client one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Each job is a named route, so you can swap the model behind a route without touching any client. LiteLLM also handles virtual keys, teams, and budgets in its open-source version.
Each route in LiteLLM's config.yaml points at a backend. This excerpt shows three of them:
model_list:
- model_name: qwen3.6 # main model: chat, coding, vision, extraction
litellm_params:
model: hosted_vllm/qwen3.6-35b
api_base: http://host.docker.internal:8001/v1

items.title: AWS 发布 TorchNeuron：Trainium 的原生 PyTorch 后端开源
items.title_en: Introducing TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium
items.summary: AWS 宣布推出 TorchNeuron，一个面向 Trainium 的开源原生 PyTorch 后端，10 月 20 日以 Apache 2.0 协议在 PyTorch Conference North America 开启公测。
items.fullContent:
Introducing TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium - PyTorch
Close Search
Blog Introducing TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium
By Nafea Bshara, Robert Hundt, Ron Diamant, Colin Brace, Rahul Solanki, Maen Suleiman, Khaled ElGalaind, Temesghen Kahsai, Cyril Bortolato, Indu Thangakrishnan, Shauheen Zahirazami, Sarang Ozarde, Adarsh Singh, Hanbo Wang, Esha Lakhotia, Jianying Lang October 19, 2026 October 20th, 2026 No Comments
Featured projects
Frontier models span language, video and audio, on architectures from dense and mixture-of-experts transformers to diffusion, state-space, world and structure-prediction models. PyTorch is where AI research happens, where the models are defined, and increasingly where production happens too. Researchers want to experiment and innovate, and customers want the performance AWS Trainium offers to enable them to achieve their performance and scale goals. The training and serving libraries are written against PyTorch’s own APIs, and new libraries and new versions ship continuously. Over the last several years, PyTorch made those APIs accelerator-agnostic, with official extension points for registering custom hardware.
Today, to address the growing demand from the developers and research community on Trainium, we are excited to share an even simpler approach to program the chip as a standard PyTorch device, ahead of its open source launch at PyTorch Conference North America on Oct. 20. AWS Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed from the ground up for next generation cloud scale AI training and inference. We are announcing TorchNeuron , an open source native PyTorch backend for Trainium, so the model code, the libraries, and the tools you already use run on Trainium. This integration builds directly on the accelerator-agnostic extension points, including the PrivateUse1 device backend and torch.accelerator APIs, created by the PyTorch community.
TorchNeuron supports eager execution for research and debugging including new adaptive eager mode with improved performance, torch.compile for production performance, and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for custom kernels, on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Also, with Neuron Explorer , performance engineers use the same torch.profiler to trace execution from framework to hardware, linking every event back to its source line to pinpoint bottlenecks and optimize efficiently. TorchNeuron will be released as open source under Apache 2.0 at github.com/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx , going live as public Beta on Oct. 20.
“PyTorch’s vision is straightforward: developers should have a consistent experience across hardware platforms. Native support for AWS Trainium expands that choice, enabling researchers and engineers to experiment and iterate using the eager execution and distributed APIs they already know. Teams can take advantage of Trainium’s capabilities without reinventing their workflows or leaving the PyTorch ecosystem.” – Jana van Greunen, Director of PyTorch Engineering at Meta
Getting started: Easy device switching
Getting started is straightforward. Run your code on Trainium using the pointer: .to('neuron') .
# Run a training loop on Trainium
model = MyModel().to('neuron') # the only change
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters())
for batch in dataloader:
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = criterion(model(batch), targets)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step() Modern code written against torch.accelerator, PyTorch’s recommended device-agnostic API, runs unmodified. A compiled model needs the Neuron backend named, once with torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron") , after which torch.compile(model) takes it, or per call as torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") .
# Run a compiled training loop on Trainium
torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron") # call once, before any compile
model = MyModel().to('neuron')
model.compile() # no backend argument
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters())
for batch in dataloader:
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = criterion(model(batch), targets)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step() Capabilities
TorchNeuron registers Trainium through PrivateUse1, PyTorch’s official extension point for custom hardware, so the standard APIs work as written: torch.nn , torch.tensor , torch.autocast , torch.distributed , and torch.profiler all operate on the neuron device. The two execution modes of PyTorch, eager and torch.compile work natively.
High-level architecture diagram of TorchNeuron ( details ).
Eager
Eager runs operations immediately, so Python control flow, prints, and breakpoints all work with no compile or trace step. This is the mode for research and debugging. Eager mode dispatches operations individually. Executed directly, each operation compiles its own Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) file, launches it on device, and moves its intermediates through HBM. We are also introducing adaptive eager mode (experimental), to reduce the launch cost and provide better opportunities to fuse operations to approach performance of compiled graph without a code change, while retaining the interactive experience.
torch.compile
torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") captures the model into a graph the Neuron compiler optimizes, and is the mode for stable, high-performance models moving to production. torch.compile can be used to optimize the whole or part of the model and works seamlessly with eager mode. FlexAttention is supported natively. TorchDynamo captures the model into an FX graph, AOTAutograd traces the backward graph ahead of time, the Neuron backend lowers the result, by way of Torch-MLIR, into StableHLO, and the Neuron compiler produces a NEFF file that executes on hardware.
The Neuron inference stacks are built on the same torch.compile support in TorchNeuron. vLLM Neuron is a plugin to vLLM and serves LLMs; vLLM Omni Neuron is a plugin to vLLM Omni and serves diffusion models for image and video generation.
Ops and dtypes
Broad aten operator coverage for ops seen across text, multimodal and vision language, image and video generation and understanding, state space models, and world models. Models can use BF16, FP32, and FP16, with integer and boolean types, and torch.autocast and mixed precision code operate as written. TorchAO and FP8 are currently supported under private Beta and will be made generally available in the next release.
Distributed APIs
Distributed inference and training can use the standard PyTorch APIs and the high-level parallelism modules compose with your model as written: DDP, FSDP2, SimpleFSDP, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism, along with common compositions like FSDP2 with tensor parallelism, ZeRO that are essential for training large models. DTensor and DeviceMesh are supported to handle sharding and the multi-dimensional process groups. The collective APIs (example: all_gather , reduce_scatter , all_reduce ) and the P2P APIs ( send , recv ) are supported. Collectives execute over Trainium’s dedicated collective cores intra-node and over the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) inter-node, so the communication transport is native to the hardware with no change to PyTorch APIs.
Streams and Events
Torch streams and events are supported natively. torch_neuronx.Stream and torch_neuronx.Event map PyTorch’s stream semantics onto Trainium’s hardware queues. Within a stream, data movement and computation stay in order automatically. Separate streams carry no implicit dependency on one another, so across streams you make that ordering explicit by recording an event on the producing stream and waiting for it on the consuming stream before using the result. The device-agnostic torch.Stream , torch.Event , and torch.accelerator entry points reach the same implementation, so code written against them runs unmodified. An error surfaces at the next synchronization point rather than at the operation that caused it; TorchNeuron tracks the earliest exception and re-raises it there with its original context. In execution, non-default streams multiplex onto a single hardware queue, so they keep ordering, priority, and event semantics but do not each get a dedicated engine; and when host collectives are disabled, a collective issued on a non-default stream keeps its place in that stream’s execution order but runs on the default hardware queue.
Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI)
The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) lets researchers and developers develop, optimize, and execute custom operators for both eager and torch.compile. Researchers can prototype ideas that require low level hardware control, including new model architectures. Developers can obtain finer performance control beyond Adaptive Eager and torch.compile by calling performance critical NKI kernels directly in model code to replace sequences of standard PyTorch operations (ATen ops).
TorchNeuron also provides Trainium optimized, high-performance operators implemented with NKI and released open source as NKI-lib , covering mainstream LLM and multimodal scenarios for both dense and MoE models, such as FlashAttention and MoE blockwise kernels, which developers can use to improve performance on Trainium. The following example defines and registers a custom NKI operator using the PyTorch recommended register_autograd style:
import torch
import nki
import nki.language as nl
from torch_neuronx import nki_op
# Declaring and implementing NKI kernels
# Note in NKI kernels, the output tensor should be defined as parameter to the kernel
@nki.jit
def sin_kernel(in_ptr0, out_ptr):
input_tile = nl.load(in_ptr0[0:128])
output_tile = nl.sin(input_tile)
nl.store(out_ptr[0:128], value=output_tile)
return out_ptr
# defining cos since it will be used in backward path of sin
@nki.jit
def cos_kernel(in_ptr0, out_ptr):
input_tile = nl.load(in_ptr0[0:128])
output_tile = nl.cos(input_tile)
nl.store(out_ptr[0:128], value=output_tile)
return out_ptr
# after this line, there is no NKI code, just native PyTorch, registering custom ops
@nki_op("mylib::pt_nki_sin", mutates_args={})
def pt_nki_sin(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
out = torch.empty_like(x)
sin_kernel(x, out)
return out
@nki_op("mylib::pt_nki_cos", mutates_args={})
def pt_nki_cos(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
out = torch.empty_like(x)
cos_kernel(x, out)
return out
def pt_nki_sin_backward(ctx, grad):
x, = ctx.saved_tensors
return grad * pt_nki_cos(x) # cos is derivative of sin
def pt_sin_setup_context(ctx, inputs, output):
x, = inputs

Diffusion at Scale: Introducing Mercury 3 – Inception Introducing Mercury 3
|

Introducing Mercury 3

Blog

Diffusion at Scale: Introducing Mercury 3
Inception Team
Today we’re introducing Mercury 3, the most capable diffusion-based LLM released to date. Across a range of benchmarks, Mercury 3 outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, while running 4–8x faster at 1,000+ tokens per second.
Mercury 3 demonstrates that text diffusion scales. It’s more than 40x larger than Mercury 1 and is vastly more intelligent, but just as fast.
Early-access partners already use Mercury 3 for voice and chat support, real-time tutoring, data engineering, and web navigation:
Mercury 3 at a glance
Quality: On par or better than frontier speed-optimized models like GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5.
Speed: 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs.
Context: 1M tokens, up from 260K for Mercury 2.5
Price: $0.20 per million input and $0.70 per million output tokens.
At launch, Mercury 3 is 50% off at $0.10 per 1M input and $0.35 per 1M output. Cached tokens are 90% off the input price.
Diffusion at scale
When we launched Mercury 1, it was the first proof point that diffusion LLMs could be built for commercial applications. The open question in the AI community was whether diffusion LLMs could scale to compete with autoregressive models on complex use cases.
Mercury 3 answers that question: they can. We’ve scaled Mercury more than 40x in total parameters, and intelligence across a range of standard benchmarks has risen 3x from Mercury 1 (mini) to Mercury 3. The scaling laws that drove progress in autoregressive models hold for diffusion too.
Mercury 3 in production
Early-access partners are already running Mercury 3 to power latency-sensitive applications such as browser use agents, interactive education, real-time search agents, and customer support.
Browser Use Agents
Agents wait on the model at every step, so small delays compound quickly. Mercury keeps each pass fast, whether the agent is navigating websites, researching across sources, or analyzing logs and tracing incidents. Agents finish sooner and have time to try more approaches before answering.
We ran Mercury 3 inside our production web-agent harness against frontier models, on 50 live Mind2Web navigation tasks. Mercury 3 completed 50% of them, significantly more than GPT-6.1-Sol. It did so using the same token volume and the same number of agent steps as a frontier model, at a fraction of the per-token cost.
Shuhao Zhang, Cofounder, TinyFish AI
Interactive Education
Learning runs on fast feedback loops, and any delay pulls a student out of the material. Mercury reasons through each request and responds in near real time, whether it’s a voice tutor carrying a conversation, an assistant grading work, or an app adapting the next question to what the student just got wrong.
Mercury 3 allowed us to give every student instant feedback without giving up reasoning. Hints, marked answers and definitions now come back in about a second, with quality as good as or better than the models we ran before. When a student is stuck on a question, that speed keeps them working instead of waiting, and it was a drop-in swap for our existing stack.
Michael Tong, Co-founder/CTO, General Learning aka RevisionDojo
Real-time search agents
Search applications start to feel unresponsive after just a few seconds delay. Mercury 3 runs fast enough to process dozens of documents and still answer while the user is engaged.
On smart glasses, an answer that takes five seconds feels broken. In our Sense API tests, Octen search took about 80ms; model generation was the bottleneck. Mercury 3 delivered the best balance of speed and quality among the fast models we tested, with a median generation time of 0.9 seconds and a median end-to-end response time of 2.2 seconds.
Kuan Zou, Founder & CEO, Octen AI
Customer support
Support agents have to answer quickly, often for regulated businesses where a wrong answer is costly. Mercury keeps responses conversational without sacrificing accuracy.
At Lorikeet, we help complex and regulated businesses build a concierge for their customers that works across voice, chat and email. In chat and voice, customers need fast responses, but we can't compromise on accuracy or getting the job done correctly. In early testing, Mercury 3 beat other models on latency while also performing higher on evals and in production.
Michael Gribben, Member of Technical Staff, Lorikeet
A real-time product portfolio
Mercury 3 is the flagship model in a widening portfolio of products that enable real-time AI.
Mercury Voice: Mercury Voice is customized for the extreme low-latency requirements of voice applications and for minimizing time to first answer token (TTFAT), not just end-to-end latency. It’s already powering agents at Audivi AI, Altur, and OpenCall.
Mercury Decide: Mercury Decide is a decision model built for high-volume classification. It outperforms Jev on benchmarks including JevBench and LegalBench.
Get started
Mercury 3 is available today on the Inception API Platform and through OpenRouter, Baseten, and Vercel. It is OpenAI API compatible, so it drops into your existing stack with no rewrites. Enterprise deployments support dedicated capacity, autoscaling, compliance controls, and configurable data retention.
Try Mercury 3 in chat
Try the API with 100 million free tokens
Read the API docs
Enterprise evaluations: we'll partner with you on workload fit, eval design, and performance under your serving constraints. Contact us .
Mercury 3 is live. Diffusion scales.

Today, we officially roll out MiniMax M3.1 Flash .
Space Bunny 🐰, which processed more than 200 trillion tokens while operating anonymously, was an early version of MiniMax M3.1 Flash.
As a next-generation Flash model, M3.1 Flash delivers a generational leap in agentic tasks, coding, Computer Use and cybersecurity, while making online inference nearly three times faster and reducing usage costs by 70%.
Stronger Capabilities Across the Board
M3.1 Flash improves across a broad range of benchmarks, reaching the level of leading models in complex agentic tasks (cowork), computer use, software development (coding), and cybersecurity.
Complex Tasks and Automation:
M3.1 Flash ranks among the top performers on AutomationBench-AA. It can complete real enterprise workflows across SaaS systems, solving practical problems in sales, marketing, operations, customer service, finance, and HR from end to end.
Scoring 76.2 on BankerToolBench, it excels at complex real-world challenges such as multi-step planning, maintaining consistency across documents and files, financial compliance, and chained tool calls.
Coding and Software Engineering:
It achieves 73.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, placing it alongside top models. DeepSWE focuses on complex software tasks that require models to independently understand code, develop features, fix issues, and validate their work through testing. M3.1 Flash demonstrates strong execution across long sequences of steps, supporting complex software development workflows at a lower cost.
Computer Use:
It scores 61.7 points on OSWorld V2, which measures AI computer operation and cross-application task execution, and 29.6 points on Agents’ Last Exam (ALE), which evaluates performance on real professional work and complex tasks. It ranks first among Chinese models on both benchmarks.
M3.1 Flash demonstrates strong capabilities in interacting with real environments, using tools, and executing long sequences of tasks—moving beyond understanding a task to taking action and delivering results.
Cybersecurity:
It achieves a strong score of 82% on CyberGym, demonstrating leading capabilities in vulnerability discovery and validation.
In in-depth evaluations by our internal security experts, the model performed strongly in code auditing, vulnerability patching, penetration testing, malware analysis, and reverse engineering, enabling efficient, low-cost support for building complex security systems.
We have further optimized M3.1 Flash’s inference efficiency through more aggressive sparsity. In everyday use, output speeds can reach 200+ TPS (tokens per second), with median (P50) speeds consistently reaching 170+ TPS.
Pricing: Most Cost-Effective
For agentic tasks, the model’s overall usage cost is 70% lower than its predecessor.
Flat pricing per 1M tokens: $0.15 input · $0.60 output · $0.015 cached input.

Redefining Capability and Cost for Agentic Tasks
Across three benchmarks—Automation-Bench for complex agentic task execution, DeepSWE for real-world coding, and Agents’ Last Exam (ALE) for computer use in real-world tasks with economic value—M3.1 Flash delivers performance on par with top models at a very low task cost, setting a highly competitive new standard for performance and cost.
M3.1 Flash is now available through the MiniMax API, M Plan, and MiniMax Code. Model weights will be released later.

Flash represents our ongoing exploration of the balance between efficiency and capability. Pro, which pushes the boundaries of intelligence, will also arrive later.

items.summary: 慕尼黑地区法院 I 五月底裁定 Google 的 AI 搜索摘要属于公司自己的陈述而非中立转述，Google 须为错误内容担责；Google 公开宣布上诉后实际以和解结案，未获上级法院裁决。
items.fullContent:
Two German courts now hold Google liable for what its AI overviews say Ad

Two German courts now hold Google liable for what its AI overviews say
Matthias Bastian View the LinkedIn Profile of Matthias Bastian
Oct 19, 2026
Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER
Key Points
In a preliminary injunction, the Aachen Regional Court barred Google from spreading false claims about a doctor through its AI search results. The system had attributed criminal allegations and proceedings to him that actually involved a different person.
The court relied on a Munich Regional Court I ruling and classified the AI-generated texts not as mere links to third-party websites but as Google's own statements, making the company directly liable.
Google dodged a binding higher-court ruling in the Munich case by settling, but courts keep applying the same reasoning. If this legal view holds up, the consequences for Google could reach far beyond individual false claims.
Google tried to overturn a landmark Munich ruling on liability for AI search summaries by appealing, then quietly settled. Now a second court has applied the same reasoning. Google's AI answers count as the company's own content, and Google is responsible for them.
In late May, the Munich Regional Court I ruled in a widely watched case that Google is directly liable for the content of its AI-generated search summaries. Google's AI had falsely linked two Munich-based publishers to fraud schemes. The judges classified AI Overviews not as mere search results but as Google's own statements, meaning the company itself has to answer for them.
Instead of hiding behind the role of a neutral middleman passing along third-party information, Google would have to own the unlawful statements its AI produces. For a search feature that constantly generates new answers, that's a legal risk that's hard to quantify. If this view holds up, it could call into question the entire business model of AI search in Germany and shape the debate in other countries too. Ad
The distinction between a search reference and original content could also have consequences beyond false factual claims. If AI answers count as Google's own content, the publishers whose texts Google uses to generate those answers might eventually assert their own claims. That wasn't part of the Munich case, but it's a logical next step. Ad
As THE DECODER has learned, the appeal Google publicly announced was never carried through to a decision. The case ended in a settlement instead, meaning no higher court ever weighed in on the Munich reasoning. Why the settlement was reached and whether money changed hands is unknown. Neither Google nor the affected publisher would comment. The court also declined to weigh in on the broader significance of its own ruling beyond this specific case.
A settlement can't erase the Munich court's reasoning
The Munich judges' legal reasoning isn't dead, though. In a decision dated September 24, 2026, the Aachen Regional Court barred Google from spreading certain false statements and explicitly relied on the Munich ruling's reasoning. Google can challenge the injunction. The decision isn't final yet. Ad
In this new case, a physician in Aachen fought back against serious false claims in Google's "AI Mode" search feature. The doctor had worked as chief physician and professor of neuroradiology from 2010 until late June 2026. On August 28, a colleague alerted him that Google's AI was explaining his departure by citing an alleged sexual assault against his secretary. When users ran additional searches using terms like "suspension," "termination," and "court proceedings," AI Mode returned detailed, multi-paragraph fabrications. It even invented a complete legal aftermath.
None of the allegations or proceedings had anything to do with the doctor. The AI had taken events involving a different former university professor and pinned them on him, something the Aachen court could confirm from its own records since the criminal case had actually been brought against someone else. Cases of AI misattribution like this have been documented before . Ad
Google refuses to delete the content and risks steep fines
Even though the doctor described the mix-up in detail in late August and asked Google by email to remove the content, the company said in mid-September that it would take no action. A formal legal demand sent the same day also went nowhere. Google confirmed receiving it, but according to the court, the false AI-generated texts were still live. Ad
The Aachen Regional Court then banned further spread of the three disputed text variants. Because the false claims could seriously damage the doctor's professional reputation, the court acted on an emergency basis without hearing Google first. If Google violates the order, it faces fines of up to 250,000 euros per violation.
The most significant part of the Aachen decision is how closely it tracks the Munich reasoning, suggesting a consistent legal view is forming across German courts. Google uses its AI to produce its own statements rather than simply making third-party information findable. "The respondent provides AI-generated search and is therefore also responsible for the answers generated in this context," the court wrote.
Aachen even cites the Munich ruling directly, noting that Google's AI produces "independent, new, and substantive statements based on an evaluation and combination of content from various third-party websites."
Google could check such statements, the court said, for example, by comparing AI output against the source websites it used. The Aachen judges added that had Google confronted its own AI with the doctor's objections, the system would have caught the errors itself.
The stakes go far beyond individual false claims
Both cases raise the question of what long-term legal strategy Google is pursuing with its AI search features. If German courts keep classifying the company as a publisher of false statements and Google keeps dodging precedent through what are likely financial settlements, that creates a perverse incentive.
For specialized law firms and affected parties, it could turn into a lucrative business model. They could probe AI search with targeted queries until the language model stitches together false, potentially defamatory statements, then file for an injunction and negotiate a settlement. These systems are easy to manipulate.
Of course, Google can afford to make individual cases disappear this way for years, since binding precedent only happens when at least one side pushes the legal process all the way to the end. But Google's motivation likely goes well beyond liability for individual false claims. If a top court were to rule that AI answers count as original content, the publishers whose texts feed those answers could assert their own claims too. In the most extreme scenario, Google would have to compensate the creators behind its sources for every AI-generated answer. That would upend the economics of AI search entirely.

items.summary: SGLang 团队推出 Low-Latency Mode，通过插件框架引入专用内核，在 NVIDIA GB300 和 AMD MI355X GPU 上显著降低推理延迟。

SGLang Low-Latency Mode: Kernels and Runtime
SGLang, NVIDIA and AMD teams October 18, 2026
Low-latency inference offers many opportunities for optimizations tailored to specific models, hardware and workloads. These optimizations often require extensive kernel fusion and duplicate code across implementations, making them difficult to maintain. To support this specialization, we introduce SGLang Low-Latency Mode . It brings specialized kernels into SGLang through a plugin framework and delivers substantial latency reductions on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. In AgentX trace replay on four NVIDIA GB300 GPUs, P90 per-user token generation speed increases from 671.2 to 928.4 tokens/s (1.38×) at one concurrent session. On four AMD MI355X GPUs, it increases from 331.6 to 516.0 tokens/s (1.56×) at four concurrent sessions. Each result compares low-latency mode with the SGLang baseline on the same hardware.
AgentX · DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with DSpark · NVIDIA GB300 and AMD MI355X.
Table of Contents
Kernels for Low-Latency Inference NVIDIA Low-Latency Kernels
AMD Low-Latency Kernels
Plugin System: Design and Integration
Future Plans
Kernels for Low-Latency Inference
NVIDIA Low-Latency Kernels
On NVIDIA GPUs, we reduce latency by overlapping dependent kernels and communication while specializing attention, MoE and draft sampling for small batches. These kernels live in sgl-nvidia-mega which accelerates both target verification and draft execution for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with DSpark on NVIDIA GB300 GPUs.
Where the Time Goes
At one request, DSpark verifies six token rows per step, leaving little work for each kernel while dependencies and cross-GPU communication add latency. In warmed CUDA-graph profiles, the plugin reduces the verify graph from 1,205 kernels to 1,189 but cuts the median decoder-layer latency from 96.8 µs to 68.4 µs. The gains come largely from reducing waits and overlapping work, with the largest reduction in the attention region. The table breaks down these changes before we walk through the main optimizations.
Region of one decoder layer, one request (median) SGLang With plugin Attention, from the previous MoE output to the output projection 33.4 µs 18.3 µs Attention output projection and tensor-parallel reduction 10.9 µs 9.4 µs MoE, from routing to the reduced output 44.4 µs 36.5 µs Whole layer, from one routing step to the next 96.8 µs 68.4 µs Medians over 780–800 instances per arm on four GPUs. Region medians do not add up to the whole-layer median. Profiling affects timings; these measurements explain the mechanisms rather than report serving performance.
Low-Latency-Specific Optimizations
1. Launch the next kernel before its input exists. Programmatic dependent launch (PDL) lets a kernel start while its predecessor is still running. It can prepare barriers, set up tensor memory and load weights before waiting for the input it needs. SGLang already uses PDL. The plugin moves dependency releases earlier so more of this preparation overlaps with ongoing computation. For example, the MoE reduction releases the next layer’s first projection as soon as it starts polling for peer results.
The attention path also uses projection GEMMs specialized for small batches and applies RoPE while loading the query to remove a separate kernel. Where dependencies allow it, attention begins gathering KV data before waiting for the query. At one request, the plugin also moves independent Engram lookups and projections onto a side stream at the start of the step. Their all-reduces stay on the main stream to preserve communication order across GPUs.
2. Publish the projection output from the GEMM epilogue. After the attention output projection, each GPU holds a partial result that must be reduced across GPUs. SGLang’s standard path uses two kernels: the GEMM writes its output, then a fused kernel reads it back, sends it to peers and performs the reduction, mHC update and normalization.
The plugin keeps two kernels but moves the send into the GEMM’s epilogue. Each CTA publishes its completed tile directly from registers to peer GPUs through NVLink multicast stores while other tiles are still being computed. The consumer starts through PDL and waits for the published results before reducing them. This starts communication earlier and avoids rereading the partial output just to send it. The consumer’s computation remains unchanged.
The plugin moves the cross-GPU send into the GEMM epilogue. Both paths use two kernels; box sizes do not represent durations.
3. Start the expert GEMMs before routing finishes. At low concurrency, routing can take a substantial share of the MoE path. With at most eight rows, each expert’s selected tokens fit in one eight-row tile. The plugin uses a bitmap and population counts to place these tiles without scanning or sorting while preserving SGLang’s top-k selections. It launches the first expert GEMM early to overlap setup with routing and skips an all-zero tile in the padded weights. The standard kernels already use eight-row tiles; the gains come from simpler routing, earlier execution and less wasted work. In the profiled runs, the median MoE window falls from 44.4 µs to 36.5 µs with little change in the second GEMM or reduction.
One matched trace pair from the same GPU, layer and replay. GEMM1’s bar includes its wait for routing, so an earlier start can produce a longer bar while shortening the overall MoE window.
4. Keep sequential draft sampling in one kernel. DSpark’s Markov head proposes tokens sequentially. The plugin combines all five proposals into one kernel launch per GPU and keeps head weights in registers while coordinating token selection across GPUs. This reduces the profiled proposal span from 85.1 µs to 34.2 µs without changing SGLang’s speculative worker or acceptance logic.
Serving results
On an 8K-input / 1K-output workload, the NVIDIA plugin improves per-user decode speed by 12–38% at 1–8 concurrent requests on four GB300 GPUs. Both runs use the same setup and simulated mean acceptance length of 3.51, changing only the plugin flag.
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with DSpark · 4 × GB300 · 8K input / 1K output.
AMD Low-Latency Kernels
On AMD GPUs, we reduce latency by combining much of a decoder layer’s computation and communication into a few persistent kernels. These kernels live in sgl-amd-mono which accelerates both target verification and draft execution for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with DSpark on AMD Instinct MI355X and MI350X GPUs.
At low concurrency, each decoder layer runs dozens of small kernels and two tensor-parallel all-reduces. Three costs dominate:
Launch overhead: HIP graphs remove the CPU's launch work, but each small kernel still costs 2-4 µs on the GPU.
Idle boundaries: Each kernel must finish before the next starts, so compute units idle while one kernel drains and the next ramps up, and weight loading pauses.
Communication stops: Each layer waits twice for an all-reduce across GPUs, with no computation running.
The plugin replaces dozens of small kernels with two persistent launches, loads weights early and overlaps the cross-GPU sums with computation. Box sizes do not represent durations.
Two persistent launches per layer
Persistent FlyDSL kernels combine most of each layer into two launches. K1 handles the mHC update, query and KV projections and KV-cache writes. K2 handles attention, output projections, the remaining mHC update, MoE and both all-reduces. Index layers add compression, K2i scoring and top-k between them. The launch boundary makes K1’s KV writes visible across the GPU before K2 reads them.
Overlapping stages inside a launch
Each value a stage produces is stored together with a tag for the current decode step, so the next stage, on the same GPU or another one, starts on a value as soon as its tag matches. No separate flag or reset between steps is needed. Weights that do not depend on routing load before their inputs arrive: K1's projection weights before the norm finishes, and in K2 the mHC mix weights and the shared expert's weights before the data they multiply. Routed-expert weights load once the router has chosen the experts.
Bringing the all-reduce into the kernel
As each output-projection tile is computed, K2 pushes it to every GPU's memory, and each GPU sums the pieces in rank order while other workgroups are still producing tiles ( push and reduce stages ). The MoE output is reduced the same way. Every cross-GPU wait has a deadline below SGLang's watchdog timeout; a missed deadline stops the launch on every GPU instead of hanging the server.
The AMD implementation is compatible with decode graphs and integrates directly with SGLang’s graph runner. Kernels are compiled and buffers are prepared during initialization. SGLang then captures the specialized execution path for each supported shape and replays it through the existing serving flow.
Serving results
In AgentX trace replay, the AMD plugin improves P90 per-user token generation speed by 45–56% at 1, 4 and 8 concurrent sessions on four MI355X GPUs, as shown in the overview figure. Both runs use the same AgentX recipe with DSpark speculative decoding and TP4.
Plugin System: Design and Integration
Specialized kernels can require substantial amounts of code. Each combination of hardware, model architecture and parallel configuration may need its own implementation. Different workloads add further specialization. More combinations mean more code to review, test and maintain. Bringing every implementation into SGLang would make the core codebase increasingly difficult to maintain and place a growing workload on its reviewers and maintainers.
External kernel libraries connect to SGLang through registration, validation, build and runtime dispatch. The diagram shows the shared design; the AMD and NVIDIA interfaces are still evolving.
The plugin system connects these external libraries to SGLang through model specifications that declare their requirements and supported configurations. Kernel teams can develop their implementations independently while reusing SGLang’s scheduling and runtime resources.
The integration separates startup preparation from execution:
Register: A plugin registers a specification for each model architecture it supports. The specification describes the implementation's requirements and provides the entry point for building it. This gives SGLang a way to discover external implementations while keeping the details of model support in the library that owns the kernels.
Guard: Specialized kernels make assumptions about hardware, precision, parallelism and serving features. SGLang checks the declared requirements before loading weights so an incompatible configuration fails early. Additional checks on the loaded model run before the plugin is built. These checks distinguish an unsupported server configuration from a supported server encountering a step outside the plugin's coverage.
Build: Weight preparation and execution resources are set up during initialization so requests can reuse them. The integration accommodates the needs of each implementation: AMD can retain checkpoint tensors before weight conversion, while NVIDIA receives a binding through which it can access runtime state as that state becomes available. SGLang builds the plugin before sizing the KV cache so its allocations are accounted for, then installs dispatch in the model's forward path.
Runtime: Specialized and general execution coexist because a plugin may cover only certain step types and token counts. The installed dispatcher uses the plugin's support conditions to select its forward or SGLang's original forward. Tensor-parallel ranks must agree on coverage to avoid entering incompatible collectives. This selection fits into ModelRunner's existing execution flow. During graph capture, the chosen path is recorded for that shape; serving can then replay the graph without repeating Python dispatch.
This design lets kernel teams ship focused optimizations without adding every specialized implementation to SGLang's core codebase. It concentrates integration work at explicit interfaces and allows each library to expand its coverage incrementally. Specialized kernels can serve the cases they optimize while SGLang's general forward handles the remaining steps within a supported configuration.
Future Plans
Broader Model Support
Megakernel/Monokernel development is underway for GLM-5.3, K3, MiniMax M3 and other models on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. We plan to integrate these implementations into the plugin framework as they become ready. These low-latency kernels show promising potential for further performance improvements.
CI and Performance Validation
External kernel implementations sit outside SGLang's regular code review process. Strong CI coverage at the plugin interface is therefore essential to verify that these implementations meet SGLang's correctness and runtime requirements. We plan to test compatibility checks, weight binding, forward outputs and state updates, including KV-cache writes. End-to-end tests will also cover graph execution, fallback behavior and performance regressions as SGLang and the external libraries evolve.

items.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 发布，多基准成绩提升且 API 价格不变
items.title_en: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 更新
items.summary: DeepSeek 将 V4.1 Flash 升级至 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017，网页端与 APP 同步更新，API 调用方式与价格不变，仍用 deepseek-flash 访问。
items.fullContent:
更新日志 | DeepSeek API Docs 跳到主要内容
Search / Fetch API 已上线，使用自研搜索引擎，支持网页搜索与抓取， 点此查看使用指南。
本页目录
更新日志
时间: 2026-10-17 ​
开放自研搜索 API ​
DeepSeek 网页端与 API 端的搜索能力均由自研 DeepSeek 搜索引擎提供底层支持，稳定处理每天来自全球各地的数亿次搜索请求。DeepSeek 搜索是 AI 原生的通用搜索引擎，索引了全球千亿级网页，支持多语言搜索，实时返回高相关、高权威、高时效的优质结果。针对 SEO 作弊、GEO 操纵和低质 AIGC，我们通过严格的识别机制进行过滤，确保向用户与 LLM 呈现权威可信的信息。使用方式请参考 网页搜索与抓取指南 。
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 更新 ​
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 已升级至 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017，官方网页端与 APP 模型也已同步更新至新版本。API 调用方式与价格保持不变，仍使用 deepseek-flash 即可访问最新模型。
性能–费用的帕累托改进 相比上一版本的 DeepSeek V4.1，新模型在各基准测试中取得了显著提升：
HLE (w/o tools): 42.6 (44.0*)
Terminal-Bench 4.0: 42.3
DeepSWE v1.1: 77.0
ProgramBench: 29.1
NL2Repo-Bench: 68.2
Automation-Bench v1.0.6: 60.5
Agents' Last Exam: 35.4
Apex Bench v1.1: 72.1
Chartography (w/tools): 83.0
BabyVision (w/tools): 92.5
ZeroBench-main (w/tools): 51.0
* 表示仅在 HLE 评测集的纯文本子集上进行了测试；Terminal-Bench 4.0 使用 Claude Code 框架测试，DeepSWE 使用 Mini-SWE-V2 框架测试；ZeroBench-main 使用 Pass@5 评测。
在提升性能的同时，我们还缩短了模型的任务运行时间与输出长度，让用户能够以更低成本、更快速度完成任务，在多个 Harness 下达到新的性能-费用帕累托最优。我们特别针对 DeepSeek Harness、腾讯 CodeBuddy、WorkBuddy 等平台框架进行了优化。请升级至 DeepSeek Harness 0.2.1-rc.1 及以上版本，以获得适配新版模型的最佳体验。
时间: 2026-09-10 ​
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 发布 ​
今天，我们正式发布 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 模型。这是我们全新模型结构系列中的最小尺寸的模型，具备原生多模态视觉理解能力。新模型结构的设计初衷是：能力上限更高、推理速度更快、吞吐更大、可扩展到更大参数模型。
GPQA Diamond: 90.9
HLE: 36.8 (39.1*)
Codeforces (Rating): 3471
MathArena Apex: 65.6
Terminal-Bench 2.1: 90.6
Terminal-Bench 3.0: 30.0
Terminal-Bench 4.0: 31.2
DeepSWE v1.1: 74.2
ProgramBench: 20.3
NL2Repo-Bench: 65.4
CyberGym: 88.1
SEC-Bench Pro: 62.8
ExploitGym: 15.3
HLE (w/tools): 63.9
Automation-Bench: 54.8
Agents' Last Exam: 31.8
Chartography (w/tools): 78.9
BabyVision (w/tools): 89.6
ZeroBench-main (w/tools): 49.0
* 表示仅在 HLE 评测集的纯文本子集上进行了测试。
API 变更 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 已同步上线 DeepSeek API，原生支持多模态，将模型名称更改为 deepseek-flash 即可调用最新的 V4.1 Flash 模型。旧版本模型 V4 Flash 与 V4 Flash Vision Exp 现已下线，出于兼容考虑，模型名 deepseek-v4-flash 、 deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp 将被暂时路由到 V4.1 Flash。
为响应广大用户的需求，我们决定在 2026 年 9 月 14 日之后继续提供 DeepSeek V4 Pro 的 API 调用服务，计费方式保持不变；如有变动，我们将另行通知。感谢您的理解与支持！
API 定价调整 随着 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 上线，API 价格同步下调。详细价格请参考 模型与价格 。
详细更新内容请 参阅文档 。
时间: 2026-08-21 ​
DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp 发布 ​
今天，全新的多模态视觉理解模型 DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp 上线 DeepSeek API 平台，这是一个实验性质的模型，用户可以通过设置 model='deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp' 访问该模型。
Terminal Bench 2.1: 83.9
NL2Repo: 57.7
DeepSWE: 59.3
DSBench-Hard: 63.6
AutomationBench (Public): 25.7
ApexBench (Pass@1): 36.5
Agents' Last Exam: 27.3
Chartography: 64.3
ZeroBench (Pass@5): 35.0
* 对于公开基准测试集中的 Code Agent 文本任务，DeepSeek 系列模型使用 DeepSeek Harness 极简模式作为框架进行测试，并使用 max 档位，topp=0.95，temperature=1.0；在 ApexBench 与 Agents' Last Exam 测评中，文本模型 DeepSeek-V4-Flash 会忽略其中的多模态元素
在纯文本能力（Agent、推理、世界知识等）方面，DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp 与 DeepSeek-V4-Flash 正式版持平。
在需要视觉理解的 Agent Benchmark 上，DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp 相比 DeepSeek-V4-Flash 实现了大幅跃升，多模态 Agent 能力已接近 Opus-4.8。
详细调用方法请 参阅文档 。
时间: 2026-08-13 ​
DeepSeek-V4-Pro 更新 ​
DeepSeek-V4-Pro 正式版已同步在 APP、网页端和 API 更新上线。API 调用方式不变，模型名设置为 deepseek-v4-pro ，即可使用最新版本。
Agent 能力大幅提升 正式版 DeepSeek V4 Pro 极大增强了 Agent 能力，在生产环境中的性能表现提升尤为显著。
HLE (wo / w tools): 42.7/60.0
Terminal Bench 2.1: 87.9
NL2Repo: 61.5
Cybergym: 83.3
DeepSWE: 62.7
Toolathlon-Verified: 74.1
Agents' Last Exam: 25.7
AutomationBench (Public): 31.8
DSBench-FullStack: 71.1
DSBench-Hard: 67.2

NVIDIA RTX Spark PCs Available Today — A New Beginning for Windows PCs
New Windows Computers Bring Together NVIDIA Blackwell RTX Graphics, CUDA and AI Technologies With up to 128GB of Unified Memory to Deliver a New Class of PC
October 16, 2026
News Summary:
NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops are available today from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI — with additional systems to follow — bringing RTX acceleration and NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform to slim, premium Windows PCs for creation, gaming and local AI.
RTX Spark delivers up to 1 petaflop of AI compute and up to 128GB of unified memory — enabling AI developers, creators and gamers to run frontier AI models locally, render 90GB+ 3D scenes and play AAA games at 1440p at over 100 frames per second, all on a slim, portable device.
Day-one support across local AI agents, creative apps and major games helps users put RTX Spark to work immediately — from editing with Adobe Photoshop and Premiere to running Hermes and OpenClaw agents and playing titles including Gears of War: E-Day and NBA 2K27 with NVIDIA DLSS 5.
NVIDIA today announced the availability of NVIDIA RTX Spark ™ laptops, bringing together RTX graphics and NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform in slim, premium Windows PCs for accelerated creation, immersive gaming and powerful local AI — rolling out from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI.
Combining decades of NVIDIA innovation into a single superchip, RTX Spark delivers up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance to run large language models and AI agents locally. On a single device, creators, developers and gamers can move seamlessly between their everyday workflows and emerging AI agents on the familiar Windows platform.
“RTX Spark brings the power of NVIDIA AI, RTX graphics and CUDA together with Microsoft Windows in one PC for creating, gaming and running personal AI agents,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Together with Microsoft and our PC industry partners, we’re bringing creators, developers and gamers a new generation of Windows PC, built for the work they do today and the personal AI agents they’ll work with next.”
“We’re building Windows to be the platform for hybrid intelligence, where AI can run locally when it makes sense and reach the cloud when needed,” said Yusuf Mehdi, executive vice president at Microsoft. “Windows PCs powered by RTX Spark unlock powerful new local compute for creators and developers, expanding what they can create, build and run on Windows.”
A New Beginning for Windows PCs
RTX Spark brings NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform to a new generation of portable Windows PCs.
At its foundation is a single superchip combining an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That shared memory allows demanding creative projects and local AI models to run simultaneously and efficiently. MediaTek collaborated with NVIDIA on the custom CPU design, contributing to its best-in-class power efficiency, performance and connectivity.
All of NVIDIA’s platform innovation comes together in RTX Spark — NVIDIA CUDA ® , DLSS, OptiX™, Reflex, G-SYNC ® , TensorRT™ and hardware-accelerated video — in a device that fits in a messenger bag. Slim, efficient designs and all-day battery life bring these capabilities wherever users create, develop and play.
From Tool to Teammate
RTX Spark gives users the capabilities to deploy local AI agents that turn the PC from a tool into an everyday teammate that can complete tasks, generate assets and write code.
Users can put agents to work immediately. Guided setup and easy installers help users get started with agents, including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy, without requiring a command line.
“Personal AI becomes more useful when it can work with your tools and help get things done,” said Dillon Rolnick, CEO at Nous Research, creators of Hermes Agent. “We brought Hermes to RTX Spark so people can put open AI models and agents to work locally on a Windows laptop, with greater control over their data and the freedom to shape AI around their own workflows.”
NVIDIA’s models and tools build on that ecosystem. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a 74-billion-parameter model optimized for tool calling and multistep tasks, brings more capable local AI to supported RTX Spark configurations.
The NVIDIA OpenShell ™ secure runtime and Microsoft Execution Containers help users control agent permissions, while NVIDIA agent skills let compatible agents work with tools including NVIDIA Broadcast , RTX Remix and Omniverse ™ libraries. For example, compatible agents can adjust Broadcast effects during a stream or batch-process recorded clips, all on a local PC.
That experience extends across devices with NVIDIA PAIR , letting RTX Spark serve AI inference to compatible Windows, Linux and macOS computers on a home network while keeping other PCs free for creating and gaming.
Create, Innovate, Play
RTX Spark helps creators move from an idea to finished content wherever they work, with the ability to edit 8K 4:2:2 video and render large 3D scenes up to 90GB, even when unplugged.
With the arrival of RTX Spark, Adobe is enhancing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, with NVIDIA TensorRT acceleration in AI-editing features. In Premiere, creators can work faster across some of the most intensive parts of post-production, from playback and rendering to effects, color grading and more. Photoshop and Premiere offer native RTX Spark support through beta releases available at launch, with Substance coming soon.
“Creatives are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible across image, video, audio and 3D, and they need tools that can keep up with their ambitions,” said Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for creative professionals at Adobe. “By combining NVIDIA’s advanced computing technology with Adobe’s industry-leading creative applications, we’re delivering enhanced experiences that empower creatives to bring their ideas to life with greater power and speed.”
For enhancing recorded content, NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 lets creators remove background noise from existing recordings and shape their voice with Studio Voice Mic Profiles. Beta RTX Video features enable up to 4K super resolution and 4x frame generation.
In ComfyUI, new RTX Video nodes can turn 15 frames-per-second (fps) AI-generated video into smoother 60 fps footage and convert it to high dynamic range without requiring per-use cloud inference charges.
Code, Test and Deploy With One Machine
As AI shifts software development from writing code to directing agents, work often spans a laptop, a cloud AI model and a cloud virtual machine for testing.
RTX Spark brings coding, testing and prototyping onto one machine. Native CUDA support lets developers run models and agents locally, keeping locally processed code and context on their device with a path to deploy across more than 150 million NVIDIA RTX™ AI PCs and NVIDIA GPUs in the cloud. Windows Developer Config streamlines setup, while Windows Subsystem for Linux provides familiar Linux tools used in cloud development.
NVIDIA Skills , an open source GitHub repository, teaches agents to use NVIDIA CUDA-X ™ tools and libraries, helping developers build NVIDIA-accelerated apps without CUDA expertise.
NVIDIA and Microsoft have readied developer tools for RTX Spark, including the first PyTorch-CUDA build for Windows on Arm, the first Python build that is native by default, the first native Conda installer, support for 97% of the top 15,000 Python packages, and coding agents such as GitHub Copilot and Pi.
Game Ready With Hundreds of Games
RTX Spark brings immersive gaming to the same portable Windows PC used for creating and developing, with NVIDIA Blackwell RTX graphics enhancing image quality and accelerating performance in supported titles.
Launch support spans single-player adventure and online multiplayer games including Cyberpunk 2077, Fortnite, Gears of War: E-Day, Marvel Rivals, World of Warcraft and NBA 2K27 .
NBA 2K27 showcases that immersive experience, using NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology with the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature to enhance lighting and material details for greater realism. A new 2x faster AI model, available today, boosts DLSS 5 frame rates by up to 1.4x. NVIDIA’s suite of RTX gaming technologies — DLSS, ray tracing, G-SYNC and Reflex — bring sharper visuals, smoother gameplay and greater responsiveness.
“Bringing the energy of NBA basketball to life means making every detail feel authentic,” said Peter Kavic, senior producer for visual concepts at 2K. “We worked with NVIDIA to bring ‘NBA 2K27’ to RTX Spark, using DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering to deliver richer lighting and boost the visual quality of materials to deliver a jump in photorealism on a new generation of slim laptops and compact desktops.”
Availability
RTX Spark laptops are available globally today from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI through their websites and major retailers, starting at $2,599, with a limited-time promotion for new Perplexity users . Pricing and configurations vary by region.
The lineup of RTX Spark laptops includes ASUS ProArt P14 and P16, Dell XPS 16, HP OmniBook Ultra and OmniBook X 14, Lenovo Yoga Pro 9n, Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, and MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI+ and Prestige N16.

评论：
感谢IT之家网友 有鲫雪狐 的线索投递！
IT之家 10 月 16 日消息，今日，商务部、科技部发布 2026 年第 48 号公告，就修订《中国禁止出口限制出口技术目录》（以下简称《目录》）公开征求意见，并对相关技术实施出口前登记的临时管理措施。日前，商务部新闻发言人就有关问题回答了记者提问。IT之家整理商务部原文如下：
问：《目录》修订的背景是什么？
答：根据《中华人民共和国对外贸易法》第二十条，国务院对外贸易主管部门会同国务院其他有关部门，制定、调整并发布禁止或限制出口的技术目录。自 2001 年以来，商务部会同科技部多次调整修订《目录》，有进有出，有管有放，已形成工作惯例。此次修订亦是技术贸易管理的常态化工作，依法依规进行，不针对任何特定国家、地区或实体。
近年来，人工智能、生物医药和光伏相关技术在敏感领域的应用不断拓展，各主要经济体均实施了不同程度的出口管控。中国参考国际通行做法，依法实施必要的管理，既防范技术失控和不当扩散风险，也保障正常国际技术交流合作，推动科技向上向善、安全可控、造福人类。
问：《目录》拟新增技术的范围有哪些？
答：此次公开征求意见涉及拟增列的人工智能、生物医药、光伏三个领域 40 项关键技术。其中，拟禁止出口技术 14 项，包括：人工智能驱动的恶意代码生成与变异技术、具有自主知识产权的细胞和基因治疗技术工艺平台、钙钛矿及叠层电池组件生产技术等；拟限制出口技术 26 项，包括：人工智能辅助漏洞挖掘技术、具有自主知识产权的通用型细胞和基因治疗全新靶点发现和验证技术、单线产能≥3 万吨 / 年的多晶硅工程技术等。公告还明确了适用便利措施等情形。详情请参考公告原文。
问：《目录》修订是否充分考虑产业发展情况？
答：中国政府一贯支持企业依法依规开展互利共赢的跨国经营与国际技术合作，有关政策立场没有改变。针对此次公开征求意见的技术范围和政策，商务部、科技部会同行业主管部门，事前已广泛组织研究机构、行业组织开展深入评估，并充分听取主要企业的意见建议，充分考虑国内外产业现状和发展需求。具体表现在三个方面：一是列管范围精准有限。此次拟列管的多数技术已明确具体技术指标，且利用相关技术制造的产品不在管理范围内，管理范围清晰、精准、有限，为企业划定了合规边界，便于政策执行。二是适用便利措施。此次列管明确了拟适用便利措施的多种出口情形，体现了分级分类的管理理念，有助于增强政策的透明度和可预期性，确保技术出口安全、规范、有序。三是实施动态调整。商务部、科技部将依法对《目录》管理范围实施动态调整，根据技术发展情况，及时将不先进或落后技术移出《目录》。此次征求意见是在更大范围内听取各方意见建议的工作安排。
问：对于拟增列的人工智能技术，主要有哪些考虑？
答：当前，全球人工智能技术创新进入前所未有的活跃期，机遇与挑战并存。此次拟将人工智能大模型、智能体、算力集群、信息处理相关 23 项关键技术增列至《目录》，主要有以下考虑：
一是确保人工智能技术安全可控。人工智能引发的各类内生和衍生风险已引起全球各国的高度关注。此次拟列管的人工智能自主驱动恶意代码生成与变异技术等，可被用于攻击国家关键信息基础设施、国防军工、核心政务等敏感系统，或用于绕过国家安全防御体系。若被非国家行为体或恶意实体获取，可能对国家安全和人类共同安全造成危害。中国政府对这类技术实施必要管理，目的是筑牢安全底线，防范滥用恶用，确保人工智能始终处于人类控制之下，推进人工智能国际治理。
二是鼓励开源开放、合作共享。中国政府致力于让人工智能成为促进共同繁荣、维护共同安全的一个重要动力源。为支持构建人工智能开源创新生态体系，对人工智能类技术开源、中国企业在境外自建自营算力中心、赴境外开展芯片流片制造、利用境外资源开展联合研发、参与国际标准制定等情形的技术出口，适用自动许可等便利措施，基本实现“即报即出”；对已通过开源、发表学术论文等方式进入公共领域的相关技术，拟不纳入出口管理范围，为人工智能技术国际交流合作创造良好环境。
需要特别指出的是，中方主张在相互尊重、平等互利基础上，与各国开展人工智能对话合作，共同应对人工智能技术扩散和失控风险。中方支持全球南方国家加强人工智能能力建设，弥合数智鸿沟，促进可持续发展。对于世界人工智能合作组织成员间开展能力建设国际合作、技术共享和规则共建所需的技术出口，将提供更多便利和支持。
问：《目录》正式实施后，人工智能大模型在海外本地化部署、向境外提供模型调用等各类“出海”形式，是否属于技术出口管理范围？
答：当前，人工智能大模型和应用产品的“出海”模式多种多样，判别具体“出海”情形是否属于技术出口管理的范围，核心在于是否涉及限制类技术从中国境内向境外转移。
此次纳入监管的人工智能技术范围精准有限，有关措施正式实施后，绝大部分人工智能技术仍可以自由出口。对于纳入限制类的人工智能技术，开展海外本地化部署，属于技术出口管理范围；如果部署在海外自有云等风险相对可控的情形下，可适用自动许可等便利措施。对于企业利用限制类大模型对外提供 API 调用、APP / 网页交互、SaaS 应用、本地端侧轻量化部署等情形，不属于大模型技术出口管理范围。
问：对于拟增列的生物医药技术，主要有哪些考虑？
答：现行《目录》中已有部分生物医药技术，此次拟增列病原微生物、细胞和基因治疗、小核酸药相关 5 项技术，主要有以下考虑：
一是维护人类生命健康安全。病原微生物技术等直接关系人类健康和国家生物安全，将其纳入《目录》实施禁止出口，是维护国家安全、构筑生物安全屏障的制度安排，也是保护全人类健康的客观需要。
二是支持我国生物医药技术依法依规有序开展国际合作。此次列管生物医药技术，对国际合作的重要情形作出排除或适用便利措施。例如，对具有自主知识产权的相关技术工艺平台，对外授权许可、利用相关技术工艺提供外包研发和生产服务等出口情形，不纳入管理范围；对于具有自主知识产权的相关靶点发现和验证技术，对外授权许可方式出口的，适用自动许可等便利措施。
三是践行人类卫生健康共同体理念。此次政策明确规定，对于限制出口技术，因公共卫生突发事件、人道主义救援、利用境外资源开展联合研发等需要的出口，适用自动许可等便利措施。中国将继续与世界各国共享技术发展成果，为增进人类健康福祉作出积极贡献。
问：对于拟增列的光伏技术，主要有哪些考虑？
答：此次拟将多晶硅制造、硅片制造、电池制造等环节的 12 项光伏技术增列至《目录》，主要有以下考虑：
一是维护国家安全和利益。近年来，光伏技术在航天、国防、无人装备、高安全等级基础设施等敏感领域的应用不断拓展，光伏技术出口可能引致的国家安全风险不断上升，有必要及时适度实施监管。
二是支持绿色技术共享。此次列管技术范围有限，其他未达到管控指标的技术仍可自由出口。公告中列明少量光伏关键设备，仅针对承载达到管控指标技术的情形。未列明的其他光伏设备，原则上不适用本公告要求。
三是完善技术出口监管制度。光伏关键技术的出口往往伴随光伏产线的出口、安装、调试、改良和升级而发生。出口经营者从事上述活动的，应按规定申请技术出口许可证，并凭证办理外汇、银行、税务、海关等相关手续。
问：对拟增列的技术实施出口前登记管理的主要考虑和具体要求是什么？
答：为掌握有关技术出口需求情况，提升科学管理水平，并防范潜在出口风险，根据《中华人民共和国对外贸易法》第十八条、第二十条有关规定，经批准，自商务部、科技部 2026 年第 48 号公告发布之日起，至《中国禁止出口限制出口技术目录》正式修订公告实施之日止，技术出口经营者在出口公告所列技术前，应当在商务部业务系统统一平台技术贸易管理信息应用登记。出口经营者应自行判断拟出口技术是否落入临时登记管理范围。已经开始但尚未完成的出口，在登记范围内。需登记的出口情形包括：向境外转让技术所有权，境内技术授权境外使用，境内技术的所有权人或者实际控制人变更为境外主体，以及商务部明确要求登记的其他情形。需要特别说明的是，对于列入《目录》管理范围的光伏关键和核心设备出口，均需按照规定登记。企业在登记中遇到问题和困难，可以及时向商务部、科技部咨询。

items.title: Waymo 宣布进军多伦多，计划2028年迎接首批乘客
items.title_en: Hello Toronto! Waymo is En Route
items.summary: Waymo 宣布进入加拿大，将在多伦多布局完全自动驾驶出行服务，目标2028年迎接首批乘客。近期将先以人工驾驶方式采集高精地图并由自动驾驶专家进行测试；Waymo 与 Element Fleet Management 合作提供车队管理服务，将逐步创造数百个岗位。官方称基于超4亿公里完全自动驾驶里程，其车辆在严重伤害及以上事故中比人类驾驶少95%。
items.fullContent:
Hello Toronto! Waymo is En Route
Waypoint: The official Waymo blog
Waymo is officially heading to Canada! We’re laying the groundwork for our fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, investing in local facilities and jobs, with the goal of welcoming our first riders in 2028.
In the coming days, you’ll start to see Waymo vehicles on the streets of Toronto as we begin driving manually. We are taking a rigorous, phased, safety-first approach starting with high-definition mapping of local street networks and testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel. This validation period will ensure the Waymo Driver adapts seamlessly to Toronto’s distinct driving conditions.
“Expanding into Canada marks an important milestone in Waymo’s global journey,” said Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana. “Toronto is one of the world’s great cities — innovative, diverse, and forward-looking. We’re proud to bring the Waymo Driver to Canada’s largest city and to partner with the vibrant business, arts and cultural communities that share our commitment to safer streets and more accessible mobility.”
To serve Toronto, we’re partnering with Element Fleet Management, a Toronto-headquartered company and global leader in intelligent fleet and mobility solutions that will provide end-to-end fleet management services. Together with Element and our partners, we’ll invest in hundreds of roles over time spanning fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and other operations functions that support our service. This deep partnership builds on Waymo’s existing ties to Canada, which includes our long-term investor relationship with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and our manufacturing partner, Magna International.
"As a Canadian company, we are proud to be expanding our partnership with Waymo to help bring autonomous ride-hailing to Toronto,” said Laura Dottori-Attanasio, Chief Executive Officer, Element Fleet Management. Together with Waymo, Element will help create employment opportunities providing the fleet expertise, operational capabilities, and intelligent mobility solutions needed to support autonomous fleets reliably and at scale."
As one of North America’s fastest-growing metropolitan regions, Toronto has both evolving mobility demands and a dynamic and growing number of tools. From bike lanes to public transit, Waymo’s all-weather Driver can provide an additional option that complements the city’s transportation ecosystem. The data from over 400 million fully autonomous kilometres driven shows the Waymo Driver was involved in 95% fewer (20x fewer) crashes involving serious injury or worse compared to humans in the cities where we operate.
Safety and accessibility are fundamental to Waymo's mission to be the world's most trusted driver, and we're proud to collaborate with leading accessibility and mobility advocacy organizations, including BALANCE for Blind Adults, CNIB, Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians, and Epilepsy Ontario, among others.
“Innovation that removes barriers to independence is at the heart of everything we do. Waymo’s history of partnering with the sight loss community to build accessible solutions is encouraging and their decision to engage with us early reflects the kind of approach that leads to real results,” said Michelle McQuigge, CEO, BALANCE for Blind Adults.
We can't wait to help residents and visitors explore everything Toronto has to offer. If you’re ready to experience Waymo in Toronto, please sign up for updates to be among the first to ride when we’re ready: waymo.com/waymo-in-canada .
Waymo arrive officiellement au Canada ! Nous préparons le lancement de notre service de transport par véhicules autonomes à Toronto. Nous investissons dans les infrastructures locales et dans la création d’emplois en vue d’accueillir nos premiers passagers en 2028.
Au cours des prochains jours, vous commencerez à voir des véhicules Waymo circuler dans les rues de Toronto, avec un conducteur au volant. Notre démarche est rigoureuse et axée avant tout sur la sécurité. Nous procédons par étapes, en commençant par cartographier le réseau routier local en haute définition, puis en effectuant des essais avec des spécialistes qualifiés de la conduite autonome au volant. Cette phase nous permettra de vérifier que le Waymo Driver s’adapte aux conditions de conduite propres à Toronto.
« Notre arrivée au Canada marque une étape importante dans le développement international de Waymo », a déclaré Tekedra Mawakana, codirectrice générale de l’entreprise. « Toronto est l’une des plus grandes métropoles du monde : une ville innovante, diversifiée et résolument tournée vers l’avenir. Nous sommes fiers d’introduire le Waymo Driver dans la plus grande ville du Canada et de collaborer avec les communautés dynamiques des affaires, des arts et de la culture qui partagent notre engagement envers des rues plus sécuritaires et une mobilité plus accessible. »
Pour assurer notre service à Toronto, nous faisons équipe avec Element Fleet Management, une entreprise dont le siège social se trouve à Toronto et qui est un leader mondial des solutions intelligentes de gestion de flottes et de mobilité. Element nous fournira des services complets de gestion de flottes. Avec Element et nos autres partenaires, nous investirons progressivement dans la création de centaines d’emplois liés à l’entretien de la flotte, aux essais sur route, au service à la clientèle et à d’autres activités nécessaires à l’exploitation de notre service. Ce partenariat s’inscrit dans la continuité des liens que Waymo a déjà tissés avec le Canada, notamment avec l’ Office d’investissement du régime de pensions du Canada (Investissements RPC), un investisseur de longue date, et Magna International, son partenaire manufacturier.
« En tant qu’entreprise canadienne, nous sommes fiers d’élargir notre partenariat avec Waymo afin de contribuer à l’arrivée des services de transport de personnes à la demande par véhicules autonomes à Toronto, a déclaré Laura Dottori-Attanasio, présidente et cheffe de la direction d’Element Fleet Management. Ensemble, Element et Waymo contribueront à créer des possibilités d’emploi en mettant à profit l’expertise d’Element en gestion de flottes, ses capacités opérationnelles et ses solutions de mobilité intelligente pour soutenir le déploiement à grande échelle de flottes de véhicules autonomes, tout en assurant la fiabilité de leurs opérations. »
Toronto figure parmi les régions métropolitaines dont la croissance est la plus rapide en Amérique du Nord. Les besoins en matière de mobilité y évoluent et les options de transport se multiplient. Des pistes cyclables au transport en commun, le Waymo Driver, conçu pour fonctionner par tous les temps , pourrait offrir une option supplémentaire en complément des moyens de transport existants. Selon les données recueillies sur plus de 400 millions de kilomètres parcourus en conduite entièrement autonome, les véhicules Waymo ont été impliqués dans 95 % moins d’accidents entraînant des blessures graves ou plus graves que les véhicules conduits par des humains dans les villes où le service est offert. Cela représente 20 fois moins d’accidents de ce type.
La sécurité et l’accessibilité sont à la base de la mission de Waymo : devenir le service de conduite autonome auquel le public fait le plus confiance au monde. Nous sommes fiers de collaborer avec des organismes de premier plan qui œuvrent en faveur de l’accessibilité et de la mobilité, notamment BALANCE for Blind Adults, l’Institut national canadien pour les aveugles (INCA), Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians et Epilepsy Ontario.
« L’innovation qui favorise l’autonomie est au cœur de tout ce que nous faisons. L’expérience de Waymo en matière de collaboration avec des personnes ayant une déficience visuelle pour concevoir des solutions accessibles est encourageante. Sa décision de nous consulter dès le début montre qu’une telle approche peut donner des résultats concrets », a déclaré Michelle McQuigge, PDG de BALANCE for Blind Adults.
Nous sommes ravis d’aider les résidents et les visiteurs à découvrir tout ce que Toronto a à offrir. Si vous avez envie de faire l’essai du Waymo Driver à Toronto, inscrivez-vous pour recevoir nos mises à jour et être parmi les premiers informés du lancement de notre service : waymo.com/waymo-in-canada .

items.summary: 据彭博社 15 日报道，丹麦最高法院维持对一名 31 岁男子 18 个月监禁的判决，该男子因持有并传播 3.6 万余张 AI 生成的儿童色情图像获刑，且不适用缓刑。法院裁定，即使图像无真实人物原型，也受丹麦《刑法》约束，量刑时不应考虑人物是否虚构；此案为丹麦首起此类定罪，并引发跨国调查，警方查明 273 名买家身份、逮捕 25 人。

丹麦最高法院裁定：AI 生成儿童色情内容同样获刑
2026/10/16 14:14:36 来源： IT之家 作者： 清源 责编： 清源
评论：
IT之家 10 月 16 日消息，据彭博社 15 日报道，丹麦最高法院维持对一名 31 岁男子判处的 18 个月监禁刑罚。该男子因 持有并传播数万张 AI 生成的儿童色情图像 而获刑。
这起备受关注的案件，涉及丹麦现行打击儿童性虐待影像的法律如何适用于 AI 合成内容。该国最高法院裁定， 即使 AI 生成的未成年人色情图像没有真实人物作为原型，也同样受到丹麦《刑法》约束 ，不能因为图像中的人物是虚构的就减轻刑罚。此前，两级下级法院对本案的量刑存在分歧。
判决指出，对于持有和传播描绘未满 18 岁者的色情材料，在量刑时不应考虑图像中的人物是否被认为是虚构的。
据IT之家了解，该男子被判处的 18 个月监禁不适用缓刑。
这是丹麦首起因制作和传播 AI 生成的儿童性虐待影像而定罪的案件，最高法院也借此首次明确了此类犯罪在丹麦法律下的量刑原则。
涉案男子曾利用 AI 制作超过 3.6 万张逼真的儿童色情图像，并通过网站和聊天频道传播。法庭文件显示，他还通过订阅服务出售部分图像，至少赚取 2.5 万丹麦克朗 （IT之家注：现汇率约合 24,801 元人民币） 。
警方 2023 年底突击搜查其住所时，男子 28 岁。他承认制作和传播图像的行为，但认为这些图像 并非以真人为原型 ，因此不应受到有关刑法条款的处罚。
去年，此案还引发了一场跨国警方行动，调查对象包括数百名购买这些图像的人。警方根据支付记录查明 273 人的身份，并在世界各地逮捕 25 人。
丹麦两级下级法院均认为，即使图像完全由 AI 合成，只要足够逼真，也可以依据现行打击儿童性虐待影像的法律追究刑事责任。但两级法院在具体量刑上存在明显分歧。
2025 年 1 月，地方法院 判处其 15 个月监禁 ，但允许大部分刑期缓期执行，理由之一是没有证据表明 AI 模型曾使用真实的儿童性虐待影像进行训练。同年晚些时候，高等法院改判 18 个月实刑，理由是 涉案图像数量庞大、传播活动有组织地开展，且部分图像被用于牟利 。

items.title: Kling 4.0 深夜上线，作者实测30秒一镜到底与全能参考表现

items.summary: 可灵AI凌晨正式上线视频模型 Kling 4.0，作者烧数万积分实测后认为其在大范围动态、复杂动作衔接和全能参考可控性上有扎实进步。支持最长30秒一镜到底直出，视频首尾帧改为最多10帧的多帧参考；1080P 30秒约450积分，720P 20秒的 Kling 4.0 Flash 仅120积分，作者推荐先用 Flash 打样再用正式版出片，此外10-bit 4K HDR 输出规格尚未上线。
